lenses.hvdc: Coded as animal characters, often as a group; disgust has no class of its own among the coded emotions, so the characters carry most of the coding.
lenses.modern: Cockroach dreams often follow stress about cleanliness, housing or feeling unwelcome; the disgust is emotion processing in vivid form.

reflect: What unwanted thing keeps coming back in my life?
What do I glimpse but avoid looking at?
Where is my resilience stronger than I think?

name: Coffee
summary: Coffee often stands for alertness, routine and connection: waking up to something, keeping going, or a pause shared with someone.
meaning: For many people coffee frames the day, so it slips easily into dreams as a marker of routine and energy. Making coffee can mirror getting ready to face something; spilling it may echo small daily frustrations or a sense of starting off on the wrong foot. Meeting someone for coffee often carries the wish for conversation or reconnection. Coffee that never arrives, or keeps going cold, can speak of energy you are waiting for, or a pause you never quite take.

contexts.reading: Often reflects a wish for connection, or a conversation waiting to happen.
May echo small frustrations, or a rocky start to something.
Can mirror waiting for energy, help or a break.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the coffee as day residue, a familiar detail through which a more personal wish slips in.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, coffee can stand for the push toward wakefulness: the ego's effort to stay alert and in charge.
lenses.hvdc: Coffee is coded in the food class of objects; a cafe setting is coded separately.
lenses.modern: Everyday routines are classic dream material under the continuity hypothesis, and morning rituals like coffee are typical of it.

reflect: Who were you having coffee with, or hoping to?
What do you need energy for right now?
When did you last take a real pause?

name: Coffin
summary: A coffin usually speaks of endings rather than death: something completed, put to rest or ready to be let go, often making room for change.
meaning: Coffins can be unsettling to dream of, yet they rarely point to a literal death. More often they mark a chapter closing: a role, a relationship, an old habit or a version of yourself being laid to rest. An empty coffin may echo an ending you sense coming, or one you are not ready to accept. Seeing someone you love in a coffin can reflect fear of losing them, or grief already felt. Lying in one yourself often mirrors deep change, rest or a wish to stop for a while.

contexts.reading: May echo an ending sensed but not yet accepted.
Often reflects fear of loss, grief, or a relationship that has changed.
Can mirror transformation, exhaustion or a part of you ready to rest.

lenses.freud: Freud discussed a dream of a child in a coffin whose hidden wish, he argued, was simply to see again a loved person met at an earlier funeral.
lenses.jung: Jung discussed alchemical images of a couple lying in a tomb as a stage of death before renewal (The Psychology of the Transference, 1946).
lenses.hvdc: A coffin is coded as an object; a dead character in it is coded among the dead and imaginary figures.
lenses.modern: Dreams of death and endings are common during transitions and grief, and often help process change rather than predict it.

reflect: What, or who, was being laid to rest?
Did the scene feel frightening, sad or peaceful?
Which chapter of your life may be ready to close?

name: Computer
summary: A computer often stands for how you process, store and share information, and how much control you feel over your workload.
meaning: Because so much work and connection now runs through screens, computers arrive in dreams carrying the mood of the working day. A smooth, responsive machine can feel like competence; a frozen screen, lost files or a forgotten password tend to mirror overload or the fear of losing work that matters. Sometimes the computer stands for your own mind: how much it is holding, what it cannot find, what it needs to close. Notice what was on the screen.

contexts.reading: Frequently tracks feeling overloaded, or worry that effort will be lost; it may be asking for rest more than repair.
Can echo concern about forgetting or losing something you built, or a wish to let old material go.
May reflect questions of privacy, trust or credit at work.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might treat what appears on the screen as day residue: recent material through which older wishes find expression.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the computer may stand for the ordering, thinking side of the psyche, sometimes running at the expense of feeling.
lenses.hvdc: Computers are coded in the communication class of objects; a crash or lost work can also be scored as a misfortune.
lenses.modern: Screens and software are everyday material for dreams; a failing computer gives waking pressure a familiar form to rehearse.

reflect: What was on the screen, and what were you trying to do?
What in your life feels like too many windows open at once?
What would you save first if everything else were lost?

name: Construction Site
summary: A construction site is something being built, often read as growth in progress: a new phase, a new self, or plans still taking shape.
meaning: Building sites are messy, loud and full of promise. Dreaming of one may reflect that something in your life is under construction: a career, a relationship, a home, a sense of who you are. Steady progress can mirror confidence in what you are making. Danger, collapse or stalled work may echo worry about foundations or delays. Watching others build may suggest changes happening around you, while being the builder points to taking an active hand in shaping your future.

contexts.reading: You may be actively shaping a new part of your life.
A plan may be on hold, waiting for resources or decisions.
You may doubt the foundations of something you are building.

lenses.freud: Following Freud's house as body, a Freudian reading might see construction as bodily change, or as a wish taking form.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading treats building as the work of individuation: the Self being given a structure in conscious life.
lenses.hvdc: Building sites are coded as outdoor settings with architecture objects; tools and machines are implements.
lenses.modern: Construction imagery may reflect ongoing waking projects, and its emotional tone may track how confident you feel about them.

reflect: What was being built?
Who was building it?
What in your life is under construction right now?

name: Cooking
summary: Cooking is a widely shared dream of nourishment and creation: combining ingredients, caring for others and turning raw material into something good.
meaning: Cooking dreams often carry warmth. Preparing a meal can mirror how you nourish yourself and others, a creative project taking shape, or a plan whose ingredients are still coming together. It belongs naturally to the book's Expansion pattern when it feels generous and absorbing. Notice who you cook for and how it goes. A dish that turns out well suggests confidence; burning food or missing ingredients may point to pressure or a sense of not having what you need. A family recipe can carry memory and inheritance.

contexts.reading: Care and connection; you may be the one who holds a group together, or wish someone would cook for you.
A plan or relationship under heat; ask whether you have too many pots on the stove at once.
Inheritance and memory; something passed down may be guiding you now.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see cooking as a picture of oral satisfaction and of the early bond with whoever fed us.
lenses.jung: Cooking echoes the alchemy Jung used as a metaphor for inner transformation: heat, time and mixing turning raw matter into something new.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a physical activity; the food is coded among food objects, and sharing a meal may be coded as a friendly interaction.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, cooking dreams often borrow daily routines and gatherings, carrying the comfort tied to those moments.

reflect: Whom do I nourish, and who nourishes me?
What was I making, and how did it turn out?
What creative project is simmering right now?

name: Costume
summary: A costume is play with identity: trying on another self, hiding in plain sight, or performing a part for others.
meaning: Unlike a mask, a costume transforms the whole figure, so it often speaks of experiments with identity. Dressing up joyfully can mirror curiosity, creativity or permission to be someone else for a while. Being stuck in a costume, or the only one wearing one, may echo feeling foolish, misread or pressed into a part. A disguise used to slip past others can reflect a wish to avoid scrutiny. The character you dressed as is often the most revealing detail.

contexts.when: You dress up and enjoy it
contexts.reading: Often reflects playfulness, or exploring a side of yourself.

contexts.when: You are the only one in costume
contexts.reading: May echo feeling out of place or misjudged.
Can point to avoiding notice, or a part of you that hides.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask what the costume lets you do that your ordinary self could not; that is often where the wish lies.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the character you dress as may be a shadow figure or archetype you are trying on.
lenses.hvdc: Coded in the clothing class of objects; a costume party setting is coded separately.
lenses.modern: Costume dreams often follow parties, performances or role changes, as the mind explores how others see us.

reflect: Who or what were you dressed as?
What could you do in costume that you could not otherwise?
Which part of yourself would you like to try on?

name: Cow
summary: The cow is widely seen as nourishment, motherhood, abundance and calm, and in some traditions as sacred.
meaning: A cow grazing in a field is one of the most peaceful images in human life: slow, nourishing, reliable. Dream cows often speak about care given and received, motherhood, comfort and having enough. In Hindu tradition the cow is sacred, and in many cultures cattle marked wealth and stability. A thin or neglected cow may reflect feeling depleted, as if you give more nourishment than you receive. A herd moving together can mirror belonging, or going along with the crowd.

contexts.reading: Contentment, enough of what you need, and a slower pace.

contexts.when: You milk or feed a cow
contexts.reading: Giving and receiving care; ask whether the exchange feels balanced.
Feeling depleted, or noticing that something nourishing has been overlooked.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might link the cow to the nursing mother and to early wishes for nourishment and comfort.
lenses.jung: In Jungian amplification the cow belongs to the Great Mother, from Egypt's Hathor onward; on the subjective level, your own capacity to nurture.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character, a herd as a group; a pasture is coded as an outdoor setting, often a familiar one.
lenses.modern: Cow dreams often draw on childhood places, farms or holidays, carrying the calm of those memories into current concerns about care.

reflect: Where in my life do I feel nourished, and where depleted?
Whom do I nourish, and who nourishes me?
Do I follow the herd, or graze at my own pace?

name: Coworker
summary: A coworker often reflects cooperation, competition and your role in a group, or a trait of theirs you are noticing in yourself.
meaning: Colleagues tend to appear when work fills your thoughts, but the dream may use them for more than workplace news. A coworker can embody a style you admire or resist: their ambition, ease, carelessness or kindness. Cooperation can reflect a sense of fitting in; rivalry or conflict may mirror tension, comparison or a feeling of not being valued. Unexpected scenes, such as a colleague in your home or a romantic moment with someone you barely know, usually say more about what they represent than about the person.

contexts.reading: This can reflect satisfaction with your role, or a wish for smoother teamwork.
Often comparison or worry about your standing; what feels at stake at work?

contexts.when: In a romantic or personal setting
contexts.reading: Rarely about them; ask which quality of theirs the dream is bringing closer.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see a coworker as a sibling figure, with old rivalry for approval replayed among peers.
lenses.jung: A same-sex colleague can carry shadow traits, the ambition or ease you deny yourself; on the subjective level, a part of your working self.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a known character, or occupational if known only by role; the friendliness and aggression counts show the tone of your work relationships.
lenses.modern: Dreams often replay recent social experiences, and coworkers appear in line with the emotional weight of work in your life.

reflect: What is this colleague like, in one word?
Is that quality something you have or want?
How do you feel about your place in the group right now?

name: Crab
summary: The crab is commonly read as self-protection, a hard shell and sideways approaches, and as clinging on with its claws.
meaning: A crab wears its armour on the outside, moves sideways and holds on tight, so dream crabs often speak of defensiveness, avoidance and grip. Walking sideways may mirror an indirect approach to a problem, a way of avoiding confrontation. A pinch can reflect a sharp, defensive reaction, or a person who holds on too hard. A hermit crab moving into a new shell can point to outgrowing a home, a role or an identity and searching for one that fits.

contexts.reading: An indirect approach; you may be avoiding something head-on.
A sharp defensive reaction, or someone who will not let go.
Outgrowing a role, home or identity and looking for a better fit.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the claws as a grip that will not release: possessiveness, or holding onto a past attachment.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading treats the crab's shell as persona and its soft body as the vulnerable self; changing shells is growth.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; a pinch that seems purposeful is coded as aggression, an accidental one as a misfortune.
lenses.modern: Crab dreams often draw on beach memories, and may reflect a waking tendency to avoid conflict or to hold on too tightly.

reflect: What am I approaching sideways rather than directly?
What am I holding onto too tightly?
Have I outgrown a shell?

name: Cradle
summary: A cradle holds new life: beginnings, nurture, vulnerability, and the care needed for something small to grow.
meaning: Cradles belong to the earliest stage of life, so dreams of them often gather around new beginnings that need tending: a project, a relationship, a fresh part of yourself. Rocking a cradle can mirror patience and care. An empty cradle may echo longing, waiting, or a sense of something not yet arrived; for some it brings grief, which deserves gentleness. A cradle in an unexpected place can point to vulnerability you are carrying without realizing it. Your own feelings about children shape the image.

contexts.reading: Often reflects nurturing, patience or care for something new.
May echo longing, waiting or a loss, held gently.

contexts.when: You find yourself in the cradle
contexts.reading: Can mirror a wish to be cared for, or a new beginning in you.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might look back to the dreamer's own infancy and the wish to be held and fed.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the cradle holds the divine child archetype: new potential in the psyche, small yet full of future.
lenses.hvdc: A cradle is coded as a household object; any baby in it is coded as a character.
lenses.modern: Pregnancy, new parenthood or caring for young relatives often bring cradles into dreams, along with hopes and worries about care.

reflect: What new beginning in your life needs tending?
Was the cradle full or empty, and how did that feel?
Who rocked you, or whom do you care for?

name: Crocodile
summary: The crocodile is widely read as danger lurking just below the surface and as ancient, devouring instinct; 'crocodile tears' add a note of false feeling.
meaning: A crocodile lies still for hours, almost invisible, then moves with shocking speed, so it is a natural image for danger that seems calm until it is not. Crocodile dreams often appear around situations that feel safe on the surface but carry a hidden threat, or around someone whose friendliness you do not quite trust. Because it is such an ancient creature, it can also stand for instinct at its most primitive: hunger, fear, self-protection.

contexts.reading: A risk beneath a calm surface; something may deserve a closer look.
Feeling attacked, or having to defend yourself sharply.

contexts.when: You cross a river full of crocodiles
contexts.reading: Moving through a risky transition, where care and timing matter.

lenses.freud: As one of the wild beasts Freud linked with passionate impulses, the crocodile may carry a devouring hunger or rage experienced as coming from outside.
lenses.jung: Jung saw the monster of the waters as the devouring side of the unconscious; the crocodile is one of its oldest faces, to be faced rather than fled.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; a bite is physical aggression with the crocodile as aggressor, and a narrow escape remains part of that interaction.
lenses.modern: Crocodiles fit threat simulation (Revonsuo 2000), but in daily life they usually stand in for social or financial risk sensed under calm appearances.

reflect: What in my life seems calm but feels risky underneath?
Whose friendliness do I not fully trust?
Is there hunger or anger in me that I keep submerged?

name: Cross
summary: A cross carries meanings of faith, sacrifice and burden and, as a shape, the meeting point of two directions.
meaning: For many dreamers a cross is a religious image, tied to faith, protection, suffering or hope; its feeling depends on your own relationship with that tradition. Holding a cross can mirror comfort or a wish for guidance. Carrying a heavy one often echoes a burden you feel you must bear, as in the familiar phrase about a cross to bear. As a simple shape, a cross is also an intersection: a decision point, or two parts of life meeting. A broken cross may reflect questions of belief.

contexts.when: You hold or wear a cross
contexts.reading: Often reflects comfort, faith or a wish for protection.
May echo a burden, duty or suffering you feel you must bear.

contexts.when: A cross on a grave or hill
contexts.reading: Can mirror remembrance, grief or a solemn turning point.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might look at guilt, sacrifice and the authority of the father in religious images.
lenses.jung: Jung saw the cross as a symbol of the union of opposites and of wholeness, its four arms linking it to the quaternity.
lenses.hvdc: A cross is coded as an object in the miscellaneous class; a religious setting is coded with the setting.
lenses.modern: Religious images in dreams tend to follow the dreamer's own background and current concerns, in line with the continuity hypothesis.

reflect: What does a cross mean to you personally?
Did it feel comforting, heavy or solemn?
What burden or decision is on your mind?

name: Crossroads
summary: A crossroads is a moment of choice: several ways open at once, and the direction you take may shape what follows.
meaning: Few images say decision so clearly. Standing where roads meet, you cannot take them all. The feeling around it matters: calm curiosity suggests readiness to choose, while paralysis or panic may mirror a waking decision you have been putting off. Notice whether the roads look different, one bright, one dark, one familiar, and whether anyone stands there with you. Crossroads have long carried a touch of mystery in folklore, as places where something unexpected may be met.

contexts.reading: You may be ready to commit to a direction.
A real decision may be waiting; the dream may invite gathering what you need to make it.
Advice, influence or an unexpected part of yourself may be part of the choice.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading would look at the competing wishes each road represents, and at which one feels forbidden.
lenses.jung: Crossroads appear across myth, linked with figures such as Hecate and Hermes; a Jungian reading sees a meeting of opposites and a turning point in individuation.
lenses.hvdc: An intersection belongs to the streets class of objects, in an outdoor setting.
lenses.modern: Choice dreams may reflect the sleeping mind rehearsing decisions that occupy waking life.

reflect: Which roads lay in front of you, and where did each seem to lead?
Which one did you want, and which one did you fear?
What decision in your life feels like this crossroads?

name: Crow
summary: Crows and ravens are widely read as intelligence, messages and transformation; folklore also ties them to death and omens, as beliefs rather than predictions.
meaning: Crows are clever, social and noisy, and they gather around endings: fields after harvest, roadsides, battlefields in old songs. That is why dream crows often carry change, a message, or something ending so that something else can begin. A single raven watching you can feel solemn or mysterious; a cawing flock may reflect gossip, criticism or a mind full of chatter. Many traditions made the raven a messenger or a trickster, clever rather than evil.

contexts.when: A single crow or raven watches
contexts.reading: A message you are about to receive, or the quiet close of a chapter.
Criticism, gossip, or your own crowd of anxious thoughts.
Your own sharp intelligence or intuition finding a voice.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the dark bird as a fear or wish about loss that cannot be faced directly, displaced onto a figure from folklore.
lenses.jung: Jungian amplification sees the raven as messenger and trickster, and in alchemy as the black stage (nigredo), a darkness before renewal.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character, a flock as a group; if they mob or peck you, that counts as physical aggression.
lenses.modern: Crows are common in towns, so day residue often supplies them; the emotional tone, curious or uneasy, tells more than the bird itself.

reflect: What might be ending in my life so that something new can begin?
Whose voices sound like a cawing crowd to me?
If the crow had a message for me, what would it be?

name: Crowd
summary: A crowd often reflects your relationship with groups: belonging or anonymity, support or judgement, being lost or being seen.
meaning: Crowds in dreams can carry you along or swallow you up. Being part of a joyful crowd may reflect belonging or shared purpose. Being lost in a crowd, unable to find someone, can echo feeling overlooked or overwhelmed. An audience watching you often points to self-consciousness and the wish, or fear, to be seen. An angry crowd may give shape to social pressure or a fear of judgement. Notice whether the crowd notices you at all; dreams often exaggerate the attention we expect from others.

contexts.reading: Often belonging or shared excitement; you may want more community in your life.

contexts.when: You are lost or cannot find someone
contexts.reading: This can reflect feeling invisible, or worry about losing someone close.

contexts.when: The crowd watches or judges you
contexts.reading: Often self-consciousness; people in waking life may be less focused on you than you fear.

lenses.freud: Freud noted that in dreams of being naked the onlookers are usually indifferent strangers; a Freudian reading asks what the crowd's attention means to you.
lenses.jung: Jung warned of losing individuality in the mass; on the subjective level a crowd may show how far you are shaped by collective opinion.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a group character, with sex and identity recorded as far as they can be, often strangers of mixed sex.
lenses.modern: Social simulation views suggest dreams rehearse life among others; crowds often appear around public events, performances or new social settings.

reflect: Did you feel part of the crowd or apart from it?
Where in your life do you want to belong more?
Whose opinion feels like a crowd watching you?

name: Crown
summary: A crown stands for authority, recognition and responsibility: the right to lead, and the weight that comes with it.
meaning: Being crowned in a dream can feel like recognition long awaited, or like a role you are not sure you can carry. The crown's condition matters: gleaming, heavy, slipping, broken or worn by someone else. Watching another person wear it may mirror questions about power in your family or workplace, and about whose approval you seek. A crown that will not stay on often echoes self-doubt in a new position of responsibility.

contexts.reading: May reflect achievement, a new role, or a wish to be recognized.

contexts.when: The crown is heavy or slipping
contexts.reading: Often mirrors the weight of responsibility, or doubt about deserving it.
Can point to questions of authority, rivalry or approval in a waking relationship.

lenses.freud: Freud read kings and queens in dreams as figures for the dreamer's parents, so a crown may carry that echo of family authority.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, a crown can signal the Self as inner sovereign, or an inflation in which the ego claims too much.
lenses.hvdc: A crown is coded as an object, usually with clothing and adornment; being crowned may be coded as good fortune or, if earned, as success.
lenses.modern: Dreams of status often follow promotions, competitions or shifts in family roles, as the mind adjusts to a new social position.

reflect: Who gave you the crown, or who took it?
Did it feel deserved, heavy or borrowed?
Where in your life are you being asked to lead?

name: Crush
summary: A crush in a dream often reflects longing, attraction and admiration, and sometimes qualities you would like to grow in yourself.
meaning: Crush dreams can feel vivid and sweet, or awkward and exposing. Sometimes they simply continue what you feel by day, giving the mind room to rehearse a hope. Other times the person matters less than what they represent: confidence, creativity, freedom or a way of being you admire. If the crush returns your feelings, the dream may reflect growing self-worth; if they ignore you, it may echo a fear of rejection more than anything about them. A crush on someone unexpected, even someone you dislike, often points to a quality you are drawn toward.

contexts.when: They notice you or feel the same
contexts.reading: This may reflect hope and growing confidence, or a wish to feel chosen.
Often a fear of not being enough, rehearsed safely; it says more about your doubts than their feelings.
Ask what quality they embody; the attraction may point to something you want for yourself.

lenses.freud: Freud's idea of wish fulfilment fits crush dreams closely: the dream may simply grant what waking life has not yet allowed.
lenses.jung: A crush can carry a projection of the anima or animus: inner qualities seen first, and most vividly, in someone else.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a known or prominent character depending on who they are; romantic moments count as sexual interactions, kind ones as friendliness.
lenses.modern: People we think about often tend to appear in dreams; social simulation views add that dreams let us rehearse approach and rejection.

reflect: What drew you to them in the dream?
Is that a quality you want to grow in yourself?
What would feeling chosen change for you?

name: Crying
summary: Crying in dreams is widely shared and often a release: grief, relief, tenderness or stress finding a way out, sometimes with real tears on waking.
meaning: Many people wake from a crying dream with wet cheeks and, surprisingly, a lighter heart. Dream tears can carry grief for a loss, sadness held back by day, overwhelming relief or a tenderness that took you by surprise. Who cried, and why, shapes the reading. Weeping alone suggests a private feeling needing space; crying with someone, shared emotion or comfort; watching another cry, empathy or concern for them. Notice how you felt afterwards. Lightness often means something has been processed; heaviness may mean the feeling needs more attention while awake.

contexts.reading: Tension finally releasing; something you feared may be easing.
Grief finding expression, a natural part of mourning, in sleep as by day.
Empathy, or a feeling of your own seen in another person; who were they?

lenses.freud: Freud observed that feelings in dreams are less disguised than images; the tears may be real even when the scene around them is displaced.
lenses.jung: Tears can mark a release that allows renewal; Jungians often see weeping as the psyche softening a rigid attitude.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an expressive activity, with sadness (or, for tears of relief, happiness) as the emotion.
lenses.modern: Emotion processing views (Walker and van der Helm 2009) suggest REM sleep helps take the sharpest edge off painful memories over time.

reflect: What was I crying about, and how did I feel afterwards?
Is there a feeling I have not let out by day?
Who could I share it with?

name: Cup
summary: A cup is a vessel for what you receive: nourishment, emotion, blessing or burden, and how much you can hold.
meaning: Cups are about receiving and offering. Being handed a cup can mirror care, welcome or something you are asked to accept; offering one may reflect generosity. An overflowing cup often speaks of abundance, or of feelings spilling past their limits. An empty cup may echo emptiness, or readiness to receive something new. Chalices and goblets carry ceremony and old stories of a sacred vessel. A cracked cup can reflect a source of comfort that no longer holds as it did.

contexts.reading: May reflect care offered, or something you are asked to accept.
Often mirrors abundance, or emotion spilling over.

contexts.when: The cup is empty or cracked
contexts.reading: Can echo depletion, or readiness to be filled anew.

lenses.freud: Freud listed vessels and bottles among receptacles he read as feminine symbols; a modern reading might focus on giving and receiving.
lenses.jung: Jung saw the vessel, including the Grail and the alchemical vas, as an image of the psyche's capacity to contain and transform.
lenses.hvdc: A cup is coded as a household object; its contents, such as a drink, are coded as food.
lenses.modern: Small rituals of tea or coffee carry routine and comfort into dreams, in line with continuity.

reflect: What was in the cup?
Were you giving it or receiving it?
How full does your own cup feel right now?

name: Curtain
summary: A curtain divides what is seen from what is hidden: privacy, secrets, revelation, and the moment before something is shown.
meaning: Curtains control what can be seen. Drawing them closed may mirror a need for privacy, rest or protection from scrutiny; opening them can feel like revelation, letting light or truth in. A curtain moving by itself often carries suspense, a sense that something is about to be revealed or that someone is near. A stage curtain rising points to beginnings, performance or a moment in the spotlight; falling, to endings. What lies behind the curtain, or what you fear does, is often the heart of it.

contexts.reading: Often reflects a need for privacy, rest or protection.
May mirror revelation, a beginning or something coming to light.
Can echo suspense, or a feeling about to be acknowledged.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the curtain as the dream's own censorship, drawn across a wish not yet admitted.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the curtain is the threshold between conscious and unconscious; drawing it back can mean meeting the shadow.
lenses.hvdc: A curtain is coded as a household object; the indoor setting is coded separately.
lenses.modern: Uncertainty about what is hidden is a natural source of anticipation in dreams, as the mind predicts what might appear.

reflect: What was behind the curtain, or what did you fear was?
Were you opening it or closing it?
What in your life is ready to come to light?

name: Dancing
summary: Dancing is a widely shared dream of joy, rhythm and connection: moving freely with your body, with music or with someone else.
meaning: Dance joins body and feeling, so dream dancing often reflects how at ease you are in yourself and with others. Moving freely to music suggests release and pleasure, part of the book's Expansion pattern; dancing in step with a partner can mirror harmony in a relationship, while stepping on toes or losing the rhythm may point to friction or bad timing. Notice whether you danced alone, with someone known or with a stranger, and whether anyone watched. Being watched can turn joy into performance.

contexts.reading: Self-expression without an audience; often a sign of renewed confidence or a wish for more play.
Harmony, trust and give and take; notice who leads and whether it feels balanced.
Feeling out of sync with a group, a relationship or the pace of change around you.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see dancing as a socially permitted form of closeness and bodily pleasure, letting a wish appear in acceptable dress.
lenses.jung: Dancing with a partner can picture the union of opposites, sometimes an encounter with anima or animus; solo dance may express the Self in motion.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a physical activity; dancing with a partner may also be coded as a friendly interaction, and enjoyment as happiness.
lenses.modern: Positive emotion is common in dreams too; dancing dreams may echo social events, music heard during the day or a longing for celebration.

reflect: Where in my life do I feel free to move as I like?
Who was I dancing with, and who led?
What would bring more rhythm or play into my days?

name: Daughter
summary: A daughter often reflects tenderness, protection and pride, and can stand for a creative or emotional part of yourself that is growing.
meaning: Dreams of a daughter often mirror the living relationship: worry about her safety or happiness, pride in her independence, or the ache of watching her change. Without a real daughter, the figure may represent something you are bringing into being, a sensitivity you are learning to value, or the girl you once were. Her age and the setting offer clues. A daughter calling out to you may highlight responsibilities that feel heavy; one who leads the way may suggest that a newer part of you is ready to guide.

contexts.when: She leads you or shows you something
contexts.reading: This could point to trust in a fresh perspective, or in qualities she represents for you.

contexts.when: You cannot reach or protect her
contexts.reading: Often love and helplessness about something in waking life, not a forecast about her.

contexts.when: She looks like you as a girl
contexts.reading: A younger self may want attention, play or reassurance that she was enough.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might explore the wishes a parent places on a daughter, and how they echo the parent's own childhood.
lenses.jung: For a father a daughter can carry anima qualities; for a mother, a renewed version of herself; either way, feeling that is emerging.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a family character (daughter) with her age; protective acts toward her count as friendliness initiated by the dreamer.
lenses.modern: The continuity hypothesis expects a daughter to appear in a parent's dreams in line with how present and emotionally charged the bond is.

reflect: How old was she in the dream, and why that age?
What did she need from you?
What are you growing that needs similar care?

name: Death of a Loved One
summary: Dreaming that someone you love dies usually reflects love, fear of loss or change in the relationship, not a prediction.
meaning: Few dreams are as frightening to wake from, and it helps to know they are widely reported and almost never literal. A loved one's death in a dream often marks change: a child growing up, a parent ageing, a friendship shifting, a relationship entering a new stage. It can also give form to the fear of loss that love naturally brings. Sometimes the person stands for a quality of theirs that is fading in your own life. If you are caring for someone who is ill, these dreams may simply rehearse the worry you carry. Be gentle with yourself on waking.

contexts.reading: Often awareness of their ageing, or of your own growing independence.
Usually the depth of your love and protectiveness speaking; notice what has felt uncertain lately.
This can point to a change in the relationship that is already under way.

lenses.freud: Freud sorted these dreams by whether they bring grief; the grieving ones he traced to childhood rivalries long outgrown, when wishing someone gone did not yet mean forever.
lenses.jung: Jung read death in dreams as transformation; on the subjective level, the quality that person represents may be changing in you.
lenses.hvdc: Death is coded as a misfortune to the character who dies; such dreams also add to the coded emotions, usually sadness or apprehension.
lenses.modern: Dreams of loss may rehearse frightening possibilities in a safe space, in line with threat simulation and emotional processing views.

reflect: What has been changing in your relationship with this person?
What would you want them to know?
Which of their qualities matters to you right now?

name: Deceased Loved One
summary: Dreaming of someone who has died often reflects love, grief and connection, and the mind's way of continuing a bond.
meaning: Dreams of loved ones who have passed away can be among the most moving we have. Some feel like visits: vivid, calm, full of warmth or a sense of message. Others are painful, replaying illness or the moment of loss, or showing the person as distant. Both kinds are part of how grief moves. Many bereaved people find these dreams comforting; some find them unsettling, especially early on. There is no correct meaning to extract. What the person said, how they looked and how you felt on waking are worth keeping, gently, as part of a relationship that continues.

contexts.when: They seem well, peaceful or reassuring
contexts.reading: Many people wake comforted; the dream may help you hold love alongside loss.

contexts.when: They are ill, distant or silent
contexts.reading: Often grief still raw, or something unsaid; if these dreams weigh on you for a long time, sharing them with someone you trust can help.

contexts.when: They give you a message or advice
contexts.reading: Consider it your own inner knowledge in their voice, offered with their love.

lenses.freud: Freud wrote about dreams in which a dead parent appears alive, and saw in them the mind still working through love and mixed feelings.
lenses.jung: On Jung's subjective level, the person can also stand for qualities of theirs that now live on in you.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a character who is dead in waking life; dead and imaginary characters together form one of the content indicators.
lenses.modern: Studies of bereaved dreamers find these dreams common and often comforting, part of the emotional work of grief.

reflect: How did you feel when you woke?
What did they say, or what did you want to say?
What part of them do you carry with you?

name: Deer
summary: The deer is widely seen as gentleness, grace and alert sensitivity, and the stag's antlers as natural dignity and renewal.
meaning: A deer at the edge of a clearing is gentleness on high alert: graceful, beautiful, ready to vanish at a sound. Dreams may use it for your own sensitivity, a shy or innocent part of you, or a tender relationship that needs quiet to grow. A stag with full antlers often carries dignity and natural authority, and because antlers fall and grow back each year, renewal. A deer frozen in headlights, or hunted, may reflect feeling exposed or targeted.

contexts.reading: A shy, sensitive part of you, or of someone close, that needs a gentle approach.
Dignity, inner authority, and renewal after loss.
Feeling exposed, targeted, or frozen by a sudden demand.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the hunted deer as a displaced fear of being pursued, or as a wish to keep some innocence safe.
lenses.jung: In Jungian amplification the deer often leads the hero into the forest of the unconscious; in the alchemical images Jung studied it can stand for the soul.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; if you hunt it, that is coded as aggression by the dreamer, which is worth noticing.
lenses.modern: Deer dreams often carry tender or anxious feelings about vulnerability; for drivers a startled deer can also be simple day residue.

reflect: What sensitive part of me needs a quieter approach?
Where do I feel exposed or frozen?
What is growing back in me after a loss?

name: Déjà Vu
aliases: felt like i had been here before
summary: Déjà vu is the uncanny sense that a new moment has happened before; in dreams, or after them, it can feel like time folding back on itself.
meaning: It may happen inside a dream, in a place you are certain you have visited, or in waking life, when a scene seems to replay something you once dreamed. Memory researchers describe déjà vu as a glitch of familiarity: the feeling of recognition switches on without a matching memory. Some people take waking moments that echo a dream as a sign the dream foresaw them; that is a widely held belief rather than something research supports. Either way, the experience invites curiosity. Notice the setting and what you felt: comfort, unease or wonder.

contexts.when: A dream place that feels deeply familiar
contexts.reading: It may blend real memories, or return in recurring dreams; consider keeping notes on such places.

contexts.when: A waking moment that echoes a dream
contexts.reading: Often a striking coincidence of familiarity; record the dream and the moment to look back on later.
Usually brief and harmless; if it happens very often while awake, mentioning it to a doctor is sensible.

lenses.freud: Freud discussed déjà vu in waking life, suggesting it may revive an unconscious fantasy or wish the person once had and then forgot.
lenses.jung: Jung's idea of synchronicity, meaningful coincidence, is how some read such moments; he framed it as meaning, not as proof of foresight.
lenses.hvdc: The coding has no category for déjà vu; it may record the dreamer's thinking, any confusion as an emotion, and the familiarity of the setting.
lenses.modern: Brown (2003) reviewed déjà vu research and described it as a memory phenomenon: a familiarity signal that fires without a matching memory.

reflect: What felt familiar, and why might it matter now?
Did it bring comfort, unease or wonder?
What would I like to remember about this moment?

name: Demon
summary: Demons are widely read as inner struggles given a face: temptation, guilt, anger or fear that feels as if it comes from outside.
meaning: Many religious and folk traditions speak of demons, and how such a dream feels can depend a great deal on your own beliefs, which deserve respect. Psychologically, a demon often personifies something you are struggling with: an urge you are resisting, a harsh inner voice, shame, anger, or an influence you feel is harmful. Seeing it as a separate figure can make it easier to face. A frightening dream like this says more about what you are carrying than about what will happen.

contexts.when: A demon pursues or torments you
contexts.reading: An inner struggle, guilt, anger or a craving, that feels as if it has a will of its own.

contexts.when: You drive it away or pray
contexts.reading: Strength, faith or self-respect rising to meet what troubles you.

contexts.when: A presence in the room as you wake, unable to move
contexts.reading: This is often part of sleep paralysis, a common and usually harmless sleep event.

lenses.freud: In 'A Seventeenth-Century Demonological Neurosis' (1923) Freud read a painter's pact with the devil as a substitute for his relationship with his father.
lenses.jung: Jung saw such figures as personifications of the shadow and of autonomous complexes, parts of the psyche that act as if they had their own will.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an imaginary creature in the Dead and Imaginary class; threats or attacks are coded as aggression toward the dreamer.
lenses.modern: A threatening presence felt while unable to move is a recognised feature of sleep paralysis (Cheyne and colleagues 1999); if it happens often, a doctor can help.

reflect: What struggle in my life feels as if it has a will of its own?
What helps me feel stronger than it?
Who could I talk to about what troubles me?

name: Dinosaur
summary: Dinosaurs are often read as the ancient past, old patterns or fears still alive, and as something huge that seems outdated but will not go away.
meaning: Dinosaurs are vast, ancient and long gone, so dream dinosaurs often carry the past: old fears, family patterns or ways of thinking that should be over but are still roaming about. Being chased by one, as in many films, can mirror a big, primitive threat. A gentle plant-eater may feel awe-inspiring rather than frightening. Calling something a 'dinosaur' also means outdated, so the dream may ask what in your life, a habit, a job, a belief, has outlived its time.

contexts.reading: An old or primitive fear that feels enormous.
Awe, perspective and a sense of deep time.
Digging into the past; something long buried is coming to light.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the dinosaur as an infantile fear preserved intact: the oldest layer of wishes and terrors, still alive.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading treats the dinosaur as the archaic layer of the psyche, powerful and impersonal, older than any personal past.
lenses.hvdc: Usually coded as an animal character, since dinosaurs were real animals; one that talks or behaves like a monster may be coded as an imaginary creature instead.
lenses.modern: Dinosaur dreams often draw on films and museums; a chase fits threat simulation (Revonsuo 2000), while a peaceful scene may reflect awe.

reflect: What old fear or pattern is still roaming my life?
What has outlived its time?
What am I digging up from the past?

name: Divorce
summary: Divorce in a dream often reflects separation, change or the end of a chapter, and sometimes fears about a bond you value.
meaning: Dreaming of divorce does not foretell one. In a dream the image may point to any separation: from a job, a habit, an identity or a way of seeing yourself. If you are in a relationship, the dream may voice insecurity, distance or worry after an argument, giving the fear a story to play out safely. If you have been through a divorce, the dream may be revisiting that loss or showing how far you have healed. People whose parents divorced sometimes dream of the separation long after, as old feelings meet new situations.

contexts.reading: Usually fear or distance asking for attention, not a forecast; what feels unspoken between you?
This can reflect family tension, or a split between two values you were raised with.

contexts.when: You feel relieved in the dream
contexts.reading: This may point to something in your life you are ready to separate from.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might look at the wish and the fear bound together in separation: wanting freedom while dreading loss.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, divorce may picture a split within: two parts of you that are no longer working together.
lenses.hvdc: There is no code for divorce itself; the coding records the characters, any aggression or friendliness between them, and the emotions.
lenses.modern: Rosalind Cartwright studied the dreams of people going through divorce and saw dreaming as part of how the mind works through such a change.

reflect: What was separating in the dream?
What would you like to end, or to protect?
How did you feel when it was over?

name: Doctor
summary: A doctor often represents healing, expertise and the wish to be taken care of, or concern about health and vulnerability.
meaning: A doctor in a dream can bring reassurance or dread, depending on the scene. Often the figure reflects a need for help: someone to work out what is wrong and make it better, emotionally as much as physically. A calm, capable doctor may point to trust in your own ability to heal or in the support around you. Bad news, a doctor who will not listen or a procedure you did not agree to may echo feeling powerless or unheard. These dreams speak about care and control, not about your actual health.

contexts.when: The doctor reassures or heals you
contexts.reading: Often a wish for care, or trust that something painful is being mended.
This tends to voice worry or a sense of vulnerability, not a medical forecast.
You may be taking on a caring role, or ready to address a problem you have been avoiding.

lenses.freud: Freud's own specimen dream, about his patient Irma, was crowded with doctors; he read it as a wish to be free of blame for her illness.
lenses.jung: The doctor can be an image of the healer within, close to the wise old figure; Jung saw dreams as part of the psyche's self-regulation.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an occupational character, or as known if it is your own doctor; any illness in the scene counts as a bodily misfortune.
lenses.modern: Health worries, a recent appointment or caring for someone often bring doctors into dreams, consistent with the continuity hypothesis.

reflect: What did you want the doctor to fix?
Where do you need care right now?
Who could you ask for help?

name: Dog
summary: The dog is widely seen as loyalty, friendship and protection; when it threatens, it may mirror broken trust or anger close to home.
meaning: Of all animals the dog lives closest to human life, so dream dogs tend to speak about relationships: loyalty, friendship, guarding or being guarded. A friendly dog often brings comfort or the sense that someone has your back. A snarling dog turns that closeness around, which is why it can unsettle more than a wild animal: something familiar feels unsafe. If it is a dog you know, your memories of it, and of your life at that time, are part of the meaning.

contexts.reading: Warmth, companionship, or a reminder of someone who has been faithful to you.
Possible tension with someone close, loyalty that feels betrayed, or your own guarded anger.
A search for belonging, or a part of you that feels abandoned.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the dog as a displaced family figure, a protective or threatening parent, sibling or partner, made safer to feel about in animal form.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading often sees the dog as befriended instinct, guide and guardian; in myth dogs escort or guard the way to the underworld.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; a bite is coded as physical aggression, a wagging welcome as friendliness.
lenses.modern: Dogs that share your waking life often turn up in your dreams, as the continuity hypothesis expects, carrying feelings about everyday attachment and care.

reflect: Was the dog a friend, a guard or a threat?
Who has been loyal to me lately, and to whom am I loyal?
If I knew this dog, what was my life like when it was with me?

name: Doll
summary: A doll is a small human figure: a companion, a stand-in for a person, a vessel for care, or an unsettling image of something lifelike yet empty.
meaning: Dolls sit between toy and person, which gives them their double charge. Caring for a doll can mirror nurturing instincts, or a wish to be cared for in the same way. A doll from childhood may carry memories of comfort or loneliness. Dolls that move, stare or speak are a classic uncanny image, often echoing unease about something that looks alive but is not, or about being treated as an object. A puppet on strings can reflect feeling controlled, or controlling.

contexts.reading: Often reflects nurturing, or a wish to be looked after.
May echo the uncanny: something familiar that has become strange.
Can mirror feeling controlled by expectations or by someone else.

lenses.freud: Freud's essay 'The Uncanny' (1919) discussed lifelike figures, dolls among them, that unsettle because they blur the living and the not living.
lenses.jung: Jung recalled carving a little wooden figure as a boy and hiding it in the attic, a secret that steadied him (Memories, Dreams, Reflections, 1962).
lenses.hvdc: A doll is coded as an object in the implements class; if it acts like a person, coders may treat it as an imaginary character.
lenses.modern: Figures that are almost but not quite human unsettle waking viewers too, an effect Mori (1970) called the uncanny valley; dreams amplify it.

reflect: Whose doll was it?
Did it feel comforting or unsettling?
Where do you feel someone else is pulling the strings?

name: Dolphin
summary: Dolphins are widely seen as playfulness, intelligence, friendship and emotional ease, and as guides through deep water.
meaning: Dolphins seem to enjoy themselves: they leap, play and travel together, so dreams of them often come with joy, ease and connection. Swimming with dolphins can reflect a time when feelings flow freely and relationships feel light. In ancient Greek stories dolphins rescued sailors, and some dreamers meet them as guides who carry them through deep water. A stranded or distressed dolphin may point to playfulness or social ease that has been cut off.

contexts.reading: Emotional ease, joy and trust in the people around you.

contexts.when: A dolphin guides or rescues you
contexts.reading: Support arriving when you feel out of your depth, from others or from your own resilience.
Joy or connection cut off from its element, needing help.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the dolphin's play as the return of childhood pleasure, a wish for carefree time in a life full of duty.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading treats the dolphin as a friendly guide between conscious and unconscious, instinct in harmony with the self.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; a dolphin helping you is coded as friendliness, with the dolphin as the befriender.
lenses.modern: Dolphin dreams tend to be pleasant; the continuity view would look for a waking source of play, ease or friendship, or a longing for one.

reflect: Where is there play and ease in my life?
Who carries me when I am out of my depth?
What joyful part of me feels stranded?

name: Door
summary: Doors are widely read as thresholds: opportunities, choices and the boundary between what is known and what lies beyond.
meaning: A door asks a question: go through or stay? Open doors often accompany readiness for something new; locked ones, frustration or a boundary not yet ready to be crossed. A door that will not close or lock can mirror worry about protection or privacy. Notice who knocks, and how you feel when they do. Several doors may reflect choices, and the one you pick, with what you find beyond it, may say more than the doors themselves.

contexts.reading: You may be ready to step into a new phase or opportunity.
Something you want may feel blocked for now, or the timing may not be right yet.
Your boundaries or safety may feel hard to secure.

lenses.freud: Freud read the entrances and exits of rooms, and whether a room was open or locked, in a sexual sense; doors fall within that reading.
lenses.jung: Doors are classic threshold images; a Jungian reading sees crossing one as a step from known into unknown parts of the self.
lenses.hvdc: Doors are architecture objects; trying and failing to open one may also be coded as a failure.
lenses.modern: Dreams often stage approach and avoidance; how you meet a door can mirror how you are handling a waking decision.

reflect: Did you want to go through, and did you?
Who or what was on the other side?
Which door in your life are you standing in front of?

name: Double
summary: Meeting your double often reflects self-reflection: seeing yourself from outside, or meeting a side of you that has been split off.
meaning: Seeing yourself as another person in a dream can be eerie or fascinating. The double may show you how you appear to others, an image you present, or a side of you that you have kept apart: braver, angrier, sadder or freer than you allow yourself to be. A friendly double may suggest you are getting to know yourself better. A hostile or uncanny one may reflect inner conflict, or a sense that you are living a role rather than your life. Notice what your double does that you would not.

contexts.when: You watch your double from outside
contexts.reading: Often self-observation; you may be assessing how you come across, or how you live.

contexts.when: Your double is hostile or somehow wrong
contexts.reading: This can reflect inner conflict, or a part of you that you have refused to recognise.

contexts.when: You merge with or embrace your double
contexts.reading: A sign of integration: bringing a split-off part of yourself home.

lenses.freud: Freud, after Otto Rank, described the double in his 1919 essay on the uncanny: first a protection of the self, later an uncanny figure.
lenses.jung: Jung might see the double as the shadow at its most literal, or as a first glimpse of the larger Self beyond the everyday ego.
lenses.hvdc: The dreamer is never counted as a character, so the coding has no ready slot for a second you; here your own account matters more than the count.
lenses.modern: Seeing oneself from outside happens in some dreams and is thought to reflect how the brain builds the sense of self and point of view.

reflect: What did your double do that you would not?
Which part of you felt split off?
How would it feel to welcome that part back?

name: Dove
summary: The dove is one of the most widely shared images of peace, gentleness, love and hope, and in many faiths of spirit.
meaning: Few birds carry as settled a meaning as the white dove: the olive branch after the flood, the bird released at weddings, a sign of spirit in religious art. In dreams it often arrives when you long for peace, reconciliation or reassurance. A pair of doves may speak of partnership; a dove that will not come close may reflect a peace that still feels out of reach. A wounded dove can mirror gentleness that has been hurt and needs protecting.

contexts.when: A white dove lands near you
contexts.reading: Calm, reconciliation, or hope after a hard time.
Partnership, tenderness and a wish for harmony with someone.

contexts.when: It flies away or is hurt
contexts.reading: Peace that feels fragile, or a gentle part of you that needs care.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the dove as a tender wish, for love, reconciliation or forgiveness, given a gentle and acceptable form.
lenses.jung: Jungian amplification links the dove to spirit, as in Christian art; on the subjective level it is your own capacity for peace.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; a dove approaching you peacefully is coded as friendliness toward the dreamer.
lenses.modern: Peaceful images often appear as a conflict settles, in line with the view that REM sleep softens the emotional charge of memories (Walker and van der Helm 2009).

reflect: Where do I long for peace right now?
With whom would I like to make peace?
What gentle part of me needs protecting?

name: Dragon
summary: The dragon is a near-universal image of immense power: in Western tales a guardian to be overcome, in East Asian traditions a bringer of wisdom, rain and good fortune.
meaning: Dragons appear in the stories of almost every culture, and their meaning splits along old lines. In European tales the dragon hoards treasure in a cave and must be faced by a hero; in China and Japan it rises from water and cloud as a wise, lucky force. Dreams draw on both. Fighting a dragon often mirrors facing a great fear or challenge. Riding or befriending one can reflect power you are learning to handle. A dragon guarding treasure may point to something valuable that only fear stands between you and.

contexts.when: You fight or slay a dragon
contexts.reading: Facing a great fear or obstacle with courage you may not know you have.
Integrating a powerful energy, passion or ambition.
Something precious lies beyond a fear; the reward may be worth the confrontation.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the dragon on its hoard as a fearsome father figure standing between the dreamer and a forbidden wish.
lenses.jung: Jung read the hero's fight with the dragon as consciousness freeing itself from the devouring pull of the unconscious; the hard-won treasure is the Self.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an imaginary creature, which counts toward the Dead and Imaginary indicator; fighting it is coded as aggression.
lenses.modern: Dragon dreams are threat simulation (Revonsuo 2000) in fantastic form; fiction and games often supply the image, waking challenges the feeling.

reflect: What great challenge am I facing, or avoiding?
What treasure might lie on the other side of my fear?
Is this dragon to be fought, or befriended?

name: Drinking
summary: Drinking in dreams is about quenching, celebrating or taking something in, whether water for thirst, a toast with friends or a drink that changes your mood.
meaning: What you drink and why shapes the reading. Cool water often speaks of thirst in a wider sense, for rest, emotion or renewal; a toast suggests celebration and connection; coffee or tea, company or a need for energy. Sometimes the body itself is thirsty and the dream simply obliges. If you have cut back on or stopped drinking alcohol, dreams of drinking are widely reported and are not a verdict on your progress; the feeling on waking is usually more telling than the act. Notice who poured the drink and who shared it.

contexts.reading: A need being met, or a reminder of one; ask what you have been thirsty for lately.
Joy, connection or marking a milestone; who were you celebrating with?

contexts.when: The thirst will not go away
contexts.reading: A longing that ordinary sources cannot satisfy; consider what kind of refreshment you really need.

lenses.freud: Freud's own example of a convenience dream was dreaming of gulping water after salty food: the dream quenched his thirst so that he could stay asleep.
lenses.jung: Drinking can picture receiving something from the unconscious, a draught of the water of life found in many myths and tales.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a physical activity, with the drink recorded among food objects; a shared toast may be coded as a friendly interaction.
lenses.modern: Bodily sensations such as thirst can be woven into dreams; by the continuity hypothesis, drinking dreams also echo social habits and celebrations.

reflect: What am I thirsty for at the moment?
Who shared the drink with me?
How did I feel after drinking?

name: Driving
summary: Driving is a common modern dream of direction and control: who holds the wheel often mirrors who is steering your life right now.
meaning: The car is one of the clearest dream images of agency. Driving smoothly suggests you feel in charge of your direction; driving too fast can mirror a pace you cannot sustain; driving at night or in fog may reflect uncertainty about the road ahead. The most telling detail is often who drives. Sitting in the passenger seat while someone else steers can point to dependence or trust; an empty driver's seat, to a feeling that nobody is in control. Notice the destination, if there was one.

contexts.reading: Confidence and autonomy; you feel able to choose your direction and handle what comes.
Ask whether you are comfortable letting them steer, and in which part of life this applies.
Moving forward without a clear plan: exciting for some, unsettling for others.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see driving as mastery and drive in both senses, with speed and control carrying wishes for power or freedom.
lenses.jung: The car can be read as the ego's vehicle through life; who drives shows which part of the psyche is currently steering.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a movement activity; the car is coded as a travel object, and the road as an outdoor setting.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, driving dreams often borrow daily routes and commutes; their emotional tone may echo your waking sense of control.

reflect: Who is steering my life at the moment?
Was I comfortable with the speed and the route?
Where was I trying to go?

name: Drowning
summary: Drowning is a widely shared dream of being overwhelmed: water closing over you, too much to keep up with. It most often reflects emotional overload or stress, not anything literal.
meaning: Water in dreams often carries feeling, so struggling beneath it tends to mirror emotions or demands that feel too deep to manage: work piling up, grief, a relationship that leaves no room to breathe. The dream can be frightening, yet it is common and usually speaks about stress rather than danger. Notice the water itself: murky or clear, rough or calm, a pool or the open sea. Many dreamers find the scene shifts over time, from struggling to floating, or even to breathing underwater.

contexts.reading: Often pressure at its peak: you are still fighting, and the question is what could lighten the load.
Points to support available or wished for; notice who rescues you and what they represent.

contexts.when: You stop struggling and can breathe
contexts.reading: A striking turn some dreamers report: what seemed overwhelming becomes livable once you stop fighting it.

lenses.freud: Freud linked dreams of water, and of being drawn out of it, with birth; a Freudian reading might also see an overwhelming feeling pressing to be acknowledged.
lenses.jung: Going under can be the night sea journey: a descent into the unconscious before renewal, frightening at first and often transformative.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a misfortune to the dreamer, a bodily one if harm occurs; misfortunes are more common than good fortunes in dream reports.
lenses.modern: Emotion processing views (Walker and van der Helm 2009) suggest REM dreaming helps work through strong feeling; if such nightmares are frequent and disturbing, a professional can help.

reflect: What feels too deep, or too much, right now?
What, or who, could help me keep my head above water?
Did anything change when I stopped struggling?

name: Duck
summary: Ducks are commonly read as adaptability and emotional ease, at home on land, water and air, and as everyday contentment.
meaning: Ducks move easily between water, land and sky, so they can stand for adaptability and for comfort with feeling: troubles that run off you like water off a duck's back. A line of ducklings following their mother carries themes of family, guidance and trust. A duck paddling calmly may mirror composure, or effort hidden below the surface. Geese, louder and more territorial, can bring a note of confrontation, or of loyalty and flying home together.

contexts.reading: Contentment and ease with your emotions.
Guidance, family bonds, and whom you follow or lead.
A territorial or confrontational situation, or a protective reaction of your own.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the line of ducklings as a wish to be led and protected, or as worry about those who depend on you.
lenses.jung: Moving between water, earth and air, the duck can suggest a Jungian image of ease between the unconscious, the body and the mind.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character, a group of ducks as a group; feeding them is friendliness, a goose's attack aggression.
lenses.modern: Duck dreams often draw on park walks or childhood memories, and tend to carry gentle, low-stress emotion.

reflect: Do feelings roll off my back, or soak in?
Whom do I follow, and who follows me?
What effort am I hiding beneath a calm surface?

name: Eagle
summary: The eagle is a widespread emblem of vision, power and high perspective, of seeing clearly from far above.
meaning: Nations, empires and spiritual traditions have adopted the eagle, so it arrives in dreams carrying ideas of height, clarity and sovereignty. Watching one soar can bring a sense of perspective, as if you are being invited to rise above the detail. Flying as or with an eagle often feels like freedom and ambition. An eagle diving at you, or carrying something off, shifts the tone toward a powerful force taking something you value, or a demand to act decisively.

contexts.reading: A wish for perspective, or the sense that you can finally see the bigger picture.
Confidence, ambition and freedom; you may be ready to rise in some area of life.

contexts.when: It dives at you or seizes something
contexts.reading: Fear of a powerful force taking what you value, or a call to act swiftly.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the eagle's height and power as an ideal or authority figure, perhaps a parent, and flying with it as a wish for greatness.
lenses.jung: Jungian amplification links the eagle with sky gods, spirit and the heights of consciousness; on the subjective level it is your own capacity for vision.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; the eagle seizing something counts as aggression, while your flight is coded as an activity of the dreamer.
lenses.modern: Eagle dreams often accompany waking moments of decision or ambition, the brain borrowing a strong, familiar image to process aspiration.

reflect: From the eagle's height, what would I see in my life?
Where do I want to rise, and what holds me down?
Did the eagle feel like me, or like something above me?

name: Eating
summary: Eating is a widely shared dream of taking something in: nourishment, comfort, pleasure or experience, often shaped by who you eat with.
meaning: Dreams of eating are usually less about food than about what you are absorbing in life: ideas, affection, experiences, influences. The setting and company matter. A shared meal can mirror belonging and celebration; eating alone, independence or a wish for company; a feast, abundance or appetite for life. Notice the taste and how you felt. Delight suggests something nourishing has arrived; an odd or unwelcome dish may point to a situation you are being asked to swallow. Often the meal simply echoes the day: a dinner, a craving, a conversation.

contexts.reading: Connection and belonging; notice who is at the table and who is missing.
May reflect an experience or idea that does not sit well with you; what are you being asked to accept?
A wish for care and familiarity, perhaps a memory of home or of someone who cooked for you.

lenses.freud: Freud treated simple dreams of eating and drinking, especially children's, as clear wish fulfilments: the dream supplying what the dreamer wants.
lenses.jung: Eating can picture assimilation: taking in and integrating new psychic contents, making them part of who you are.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a physical activity, with food recorded among the objects; sharing a meal may be coded as a friendly interaction.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, eating dreams often draw on recent meals, social occasions and bodily states such as hunger during sleep.

reflect: What am I taking in from my life right now?
Who was I eating with?
Did the food feel nourishing, comforting or strange?

name: Eggs
summary: Eggs carry potential and fragility: new beginnings, ideas not yet hatched, and something precious that needs careful handling.
meaning: An egg holds a life or possibility that has not yet emerged, so dreams of eggs often gather around beginnings: a plan, a relationship, a creative idea, sometimes a hope about family. Their fragility matters. Cracked or dropped eggs can echo fear that something new will not survive, or a sense of walking on eggshells around someone. An egg hatching may mirror something finally ready to emerge. A nest full of eggs can speak of abundance, or of too many projects at once.

contexts.reading: Often mirrors an idea, project or change finally emerging.
May echo fear of fragile plans failing, or tension with someone.
Can reflect a delicate situation you are handling with care.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might connect eggs with fertility, birth and early questions about where life comes from.
lenses.jung: In myth and alchemy the egg holds a world or a treasure in potential; on the subjective level it can picture the Self before it unfolds.
lenses.hvdc: Eggs are coded in the food class of objects; breaking them by accident can be coded as a misfortune.
lenses.modern: Images of fragility often accompany new beginnings, when hope and worry about the future run together.

reflect: What do you feel is about to hatch in your life?
Were the eggs safe, or at risk?
Where are you walking on eggshells?

name: Elephant
summary: Elephants are widely read as images of memory, patience and steady strength, and of the bonds that hold a family or group together.
meaning: An elephant brings scale: something large, old and slow to move. Many dreamers find that steadying, a reminder of strength they already carry or of a group that protects its own. For others the same size feels heavy, like the problem everyone keeps stepping around. Notice how close you are and how it moves: a calm herd often reflects belonging, while one elephant pressed against the walls may point to something too big for the space you have given it.

contexts.reading: Often a sense of being held by something patient and wise, an inner steadiness you can lean on.
Something powerful may feel out of control, or a feeling you have kept quiet is gathering force.

contexts.when: A mother and calf, or a herd
contexts.reading: Usually about family, protection and memory: who looks after whom, and who your herd is.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see a towering figure from childhood, a parent seen from below, displaced onto a safer animal form.
lenses.jung: Jung saw animals as images of instinct; a calm elephant can embody the slow, grounded wisdom of the Self, a raging one an instinct long ignored.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character, a herd as a group; animals are far more common in children's dreams than in adults'.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, an elephant often carries a waking load; its calm or menace mirrors how that load feels.

reflect: What is the biggest thing in my life right now that nobody names?
Where do I feel steady and patient, and where weighed down?
Who is my herd, and do I feel part of it?

name: Elevator
summary: An elevator moves you between levels without your own effort, so it is often read as change you ride rather than steer, with all the hope or worry that brings.
meaning: Unlike stairs, an elevator does the climbing for you, and in dreams it often carries feelings about control. Rising smoothly may reflect advancement or support you did not have to fight for. Dropping suddenly, shooting past your floor or moving sideways can mirror the sense that circumstances are deciding where you end up. Who presses the buttons matters. If the doors open on an unexpected floor, notice what waits there: the dream may be showing a level of life you did not plan to visit.

contexts.reading: You may feel carried upward by circumstances, support or a new opportunity.
Something in your life may be moving faster than you can steer.
You may find yourself in a situation or role you did not choose.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might extend his view of rising and falling on stairs to the elevator, and look for the excitement or fear in being carried.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading asks which level the elevator delivers you to, consciousness above or deeper layers below, and who controls the descent.
lenses.hvdc: Treated as part of a building's architecture in an indoor setting; a fall or breakdown is coded as a misfortune.
lenses.modern: Though a modern image, the elevator fits the old dream patterns of ascent and descent, and often marks concern about control.

reflect: Who was pressing the buttons?
Where did you want to go, and where did you arrive?
In what part of life do you feel carried rather than in charge?

name: End of the World
summary: Dreams of the world ending are dramatic and fairly common. They usually mirror a big change, an ending in your own life or worry about the news, not a forecast.
meaning: Fire in the sky, waves over cities, the ground splitting: apocalyptic dreams can be overwhelming, yet they tend to speak about a personal world rather than the planet. A relationship ending, a move, a loss, a job change or a period of anxious news can all feel like the end of how things were. Notice what you did as the world ended. Many dreamers look for loved ones, help strangers or simply watch in awe, and those choices say much about what matters to you. Some describe calm or even relief, as if an old order needed to fall.

contexts.reading: Your priorities in a moment of change; the people you looked for may be those you most need now.
Acceptance of an ending, or a sense that something old is ready to give way.
An image of renewal after upheaval: life continuing in a different form.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see world destruction as a large-scale picture of inner upheaval, or of anger too vast to admit directly.
lenses.jung: Jungians read world-ending images as the collapse of an old attitude before a new one can form.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a misfortune, an environmental threat to the dreamer and others; settings are often outdoor and distorted.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, such dreams may rise with frightening news or big transitions; if they recur and disturb sleep, talking with a professional can help.

reflect: What in my life feels as though it is ending?
What did I do, or look for, as the world ended?
What might a new world look like after this change?

name: Enemy
summary: An enemy often embodies conflict, threat or rivalry, and sometimes a part of yourself that you oppose or reject.
meaning: An enemy in a dream can be a real person you are at odds with, an imagined foe, or a nameless opponent. Real enemies often appear when a conflict is unresolved and still occupying your thoughts. Imagined ones may give a face to pressure, fear or competition. It is also worth asking whether the enemy has qualities you dislike in yourself, because dreams sometimes fight inner battles in outer form. Notice how the conflict ends. Defeating the enemy, making peace or coming to understand them each suggest a different direction.

contexts.reading: Often growing confidence, or readiness to face a real conflict.
This may reflect a situation that feels too big, or a fear you have not yet faced.

contexts.when: You make peace or see their side
contexts.reading: A sign of resolution, or of accepting a disowned part of yourself.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might look for hostility the dreamer cannot admit by day, or a loved person disguised as an enemy because feelings toward them are mixed.
lenses.jung: An enemy, especially of your own sex, is a classic carrier of the shadow: what you reject in yourself, seen first in someone else.
lenses.hvdc: Coded by sex, age and identity; aggression is coded by level, from hostile feelings to physical attack, noting who starts it and who receives it.
lenses.modern: Threat simulation theory expects conflict to be frequent in dreams, and continuity research shows real conflicts carried into dream life.

reflect: What does the enemy want?
Which of their traits do you dislike most?
Is there any part of that trait in you?

name: Escalator
summary: An escalator carries you up or down at a steady pace, often read as gradual progress, or decline, happening with little effort of your own.
