Notice who was there and who was missing. Guests from different parts of your life, mixed in one room, can point to a period when roles and relationships are being rearranged. The occasion, if there was one, often carries a clue.

contexts.reading: Joy and belonging; a wish for, or reflection of, a lively social life.

contexts.when: Feeling left out at the party
contexts.reading: Fear of exclusion or of not fitting in; ask where you want to feel more included.
Responsibility for others' happiness; what would make it easier to enjoy yourself?

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the party as permission for pleasures usually restrained, the festive setting excusing desires the dreamer keeps in check.
lenses.jung: A gathering can picture the many parts of the psyche in one room; on the subjective level, each guest may carry a quality of your own.
lenses.hvdc: Guests are coded as characters, often a group; friendly exchanges are coded as friendliness, and joy as happiness.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, party dreams often follow social events or their absence; social themes are a large part of everyday dream content.

reflect: How did I feel among the people there?
Who was present, and who was missing?
What would I like to celebrate in my life?

name: Passport
summary: A passport is proof of identity and the right to cross borders: who you are, where you belong, and whether you can move into new territory.
meaning: A passport bundles two big questions: who am I, and am I allowed to go? Losing one in a dream often echoes anxiety about identity or belonging during a transition: a new job, a move, a changing relationship. An expired passport may mirror a sense that an old version of yourself no longer opens doors. A photo that is not you can raise questions about how others see you. Getting through border control with ease may reflect confidence in a new chapter.

contexts.reading: Often reflects anxiety about identity or belonging during change.
May echo an outdated self-image, or a role you have outgrown.
Can mirror uncertainty about how you are seen, or who you are becoming.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask what border you wish to cross, and what authority you fear will stop you.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, a passport can be a document of the persona; individuation asks whether it still matches the person.
lenses.hvdc: A passport is coded as an object; losing it can be coded as a misfortune, and a named foreign place as a geographical setting.
lenses.modern: Travel, paperwork and identity checks are stressful waking experiences that dreams readily rehearse.

reflect: Where were you trying to go?
Did the passport show who you really are?
What new territory in your life needs a sense of permission?

name: Path
summary: A path is a personal way through the world, smaller than a road, often read as your own route, choices and pace.
meaning: Paths are made by walking: someone went this way before, or you are making the way as you go. In dreams a path often feels more personal than a road, a route through your own life rather than a public highway. A clear path can mirror a sense of purpose; an overgrown or vanishing one, uncertainty or the need to find your own way. Narrow paths along heights suggest risk, while a path through a garden or forest may invite you to slow down and notice.

contexts.reading: You may be following a direction that feels reliable, perhaps one others have walked.
You may need to trust your own judgement where there is no map.
A choice may be approaching; notice which way feels right.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask whose footsteps made the path, and what wish draws you along it.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading sees the path as the way of individuation, unique to each person and sometimes leaving the well-trodden road.
lenses.hvdc: Like roads and streets, a path is coded as a way of travel, in an outdoor setting.
lenses.modern: Walking routes in dreams draw on spatial memory; how easy the path feels may reflect how manageable a waking situation seems.

reflect: Who made this path, you or someone before you?
How sure were you of the way?
Where in your life are you making a path as you go?

name: Peacock
summary: The peacock is commonly linked with beauty, display and confidence, and sometimes with vanity or the wish to be admired.
meaning: A peacock opening its tail is display in its purest form, so the image tends to raise questions about being seen. If you admire it, the dream may reflect delight in beauty or confidence in your own gifts. If it seems showy or shrill, it may mirror discomfort with vanity, yours or someone else's. A peacock that never opens its tail can point to talents held back. In early Christian art the peacock stood for immortality and renewal.

contexts.reading: Confidence, a wish to be seen, or pride in something you have done.
Unease with showing off, or with someone's demand for attention.
Gifts you have not yet shown; ask what keeps them folded.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the display as a wish to be admired, perhaps an old wish for a parent's attention, given a splendid disguise.
lenses.jung: Jung discussed the peacock's tail (cauda pavonis) in alchemy, a burst of colours marking a turning point in inner transformation.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; display alone involves no interaction, so the dream is coded through your emotions and activities around it.
lenses.modern: Peacock dreams often come in seasons of visibility, a presentation, a new role, a busy social feed, when self-image is being processed.

reflect: Do I want to be seen more, or less, right now?
Where am I hiding my colours?
Did the display feel joyful or uncomfortable to me?

name: Pen
summary: A pen is about expression and agency: putting your thoughts into words, signing your name, making your mark.
meaning: A pen asks whether you feel able to say what you mean and put your name to it. Writing fluently can mirror confidence in your own voice; a pen that will not write, or ink that runs out mid-sentence, is a frequent frustration image, often tied to feeling unprepared or unable to express yourself. Signing something may point to a commitment you are weighing. Who held the pen, and who decided what was written, can say a lot about authorship in your life.

contexts.reading: Often echoes a block in expression, or worry about being unprepared when it counts.
May point to a decision or commitment; notice whether you felt sure or pressed.
Can reflect a sense that someone else is writing your story or speaking for you.

lenses.freud: Freud included pencils and pen-holders among the elongated objects he read as male symbols; today that is one reading among many.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the pen can stand for the creative function: the ego's ability to give form to what rises from within.
lenses.hvdc: A pen is coded in the communication class of objects; failing to write despite trying can count as a failure.
lenses.modern: Writing is rare in dreams compared with waking life (Hartmann 2000), so a pen often belongs to a charged moment, such as an exam or a contract.

reflect: What were you trying to write, and for whom?
Did the words come easily, or not at all?
Where in your life do you want to write your own part?

name: Penguin
summary: Penguins are often read as community, endurance and devotion, and as being at home in harsh conditions others avoid.
meaning: Penguins cannot fly, yet they swim like arrows and survive the coldest places on earth by huddling together, taking turns at the windy edge. Dream penguins often bring themes of community, shared endurance and loyalty to partner or family. Their waddle can be comic, a reminder that you can be graceful in one element and clumsy in another. A penguin alone on the ice may mirror isolation, or the search for your group.

contexts.reading: Community and shared endurance; support through a harsh time.
Feeling awkward in one setting, though you may shine in another.
Isolation, or a search for where you belong.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the huddle as a wish for warmth and closeness, and the cold as emotional distance felt in waking life.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see adaptation: instinct turning a limitation, not flying, into mastery of another element.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character, a colony as a group; an icy landscape is coded as an outdoor, usually unfamiliar, setting.
lenses.modern: Penguin dreams often follow nature films or cold-weather travel; their tone tends to reflect warmth, humour or isolation in waking life.

reflect: Who huddles with me when things get cold?
Where am I clumsy, and where do I glide?
Do I take turns at the windy edge, or am I always there?

name: Performing
summary: Performing before an audience is a widely shared dream of visibility: being seen, judged or applauded for what you can do.
meaning: Whether you are acting, playing an instrument or dancing in a spotlight, performance dreams are about being seen. They may carry the thrill of recognition or the dread of exposure, sometimes both in one scene. Ask how the audience responded and how you felt in your own skin. Applause can reflect a wish for acknowledgement; silence or walkouts may mirror fear of disappointing people. Many performance dreams come when life asks you to step into a role, new or old, and play it convincingly.

contexts.reading: Confidence or a wish for recognition; it may also show a talent you underplay by day.

contexts.when: You do not know your part
contexts.reading: Overlaps with being unprepared: a role you feel pushed into before you are ready.

contexts.when: The seats are empty, or people leave
contexts.reading: Can reflect feeling unseen, or effort that goes unnoticed by the people who matter to you.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see exhibitionistic pleasure and its counterweight, shame, both rooted in the childhood wish to be admired.
lenses.jung: Performance highlights the persona, the role we play for others; the dream may ask how closely that role fits who you are.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an activity, often expressive or verbal; audience reactions are coded as interactions, friendly when they applaud, aggressive when they jeer.
lenses.modern: Social evaluation is a strong source of emotion, and the continuity hypothesis expects performance dreams before exams, interviews or real shows.

reflect: Where in my life am I playing a role right now?
What did I want the audience to feel?
How would it feel to perform only for myself?

name: Pet
summary: A pet is commonly read as unconditional love, companionship and responsibility, and a pet that has died as a bond that continues.
meaning: A pet in a dream usually speaks less about its species than about the bond: comfort, routine, loyalty, the one who was always glad to see you. A pet you have now may carry everyday feelings about care and attachment. A childhood pet often brings back the whole atmosphere of that time. Many people dream of a pet that has died, and such dreams often feel comforting, a way of continuing the bond. Forgetting to feed a pet often mirrors worry about a neglected responsibility.

contexts.when: A pet that has died visits you
contexts.reading: A continuing bond; the dream may be offering comfort, or a chance to say goodbye.
Worry about neglecting a responsibility, a relationship or your own needs.
Fear of losing something you love, or a sense that comfort is out of reach.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the forgotten pet as guilt about a neglected duty, or the pet as a stand-in for a family member.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level the pet is instinct you have befriended; neglecting it may mean neglecting your own natural needs.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; affection with your pet is coded as friendliness, and your home as a familiar setting.
lenses.modern: Animals that share our lives often appear in our dreams, as continuity predicts, and dreams of a pet that has died can be part of healthy grieving.

reflect: What did this pet give me that I still need?
What responsibility am I worried about neglecting?
If my pet has died, what would I like to say to it?

name: Phoenix
summary: The phoenix is a widely known image of renewal: the bird that burns and rises again from its own ashes.
meaning: In classical legend the phoenix lived for centuries, burned on its own pyre and was reborn from the ashes; similar fire birds appear in other traditions. In dreams it most often comes during or after something that feels like an ending: a loss, a breakdown, burnout, a life change. The phoenix does not deny the fire; it says that something can come through it. Seeing one rise may bring hope; being the phoenix can reflect a deep sense of your own resilience.

contexts.reading: Renewal after an ending; something new is becoming possible.
A painful letting go that may be part of transformation.
Your own resilience and capacity to begin again.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the phoenix as a wish that loss can be undone, a refusal of endings dressed in fire.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading sees death and rebirth, the transformation at the heart of individuation; alchemical imagery also used the phoenix for renewal.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an imaginary creature, which counts toward the Dead and Imaginary indicator; setting and emotion carry most of the coding.
lenses.modern: Phoenix dreams often come after hardship, consistent with the idea that dreaming helps process difficult emotion and shape a story of recovery.

reflect: What has ended or burned down in my life?
What might be rising from it?
Where have I already begun again?

name: Phone
summary: A phone stands for connection: reaching someone, being reached, and the worry of missing a message that matters.
meaning: Phones now appear often in dreams, which makes sense: they sit at the center of how we connect, plan and wait. In sleep they usually carry relational feeling. A call from someone you miss can feel like real contact; a screen that will not unlock or a number that keeps misdialing is a well-known frustration dream, often tied to feeling unheard or unable to reach help. Note who you were trying to reach, and what you hoped to say.

contexts.when: You cannot dial, or the screen fails
contexts.reading: A common frustration theme; it may echo feeling unable to get through to someone, or to get help in time.

contexts.when: A call or message from someone absent
contexts.reading: Often carries longing or an unfinished conversation, especially with people you have lost or drifted from.

contexts.when: You lose or break your phone
contexts.reading: Can mirror worry about being cut off, or sometimes a quiet wish to be unreachable for a while.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask whose voice you wished to hear, and what the message would have allowed you to say.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, a phone call can be contact with an inner voice: a part of you trying to get through.
lenses.hvdc: Phones are coded in the communication class of objects; who calls whom also shapes the interaction codes.
lenses.modern: Continuity is strong here: daily phone habits feed dreams directly, and a failing phone gives shape to waking frustration about reaching people.

reflect: Who were you trying to reach, or who was trying to reach you?
What did you want to say that you could not?
Where in waking life do you feel hard to reach, or unheard?

name: Phone Call
summary: A phone call in a dream is about connection and messages: someone trying to reach you, or you trying to reach them.
meaning: Who calls, and what they say, carries the meaning. A call from a friend may mirror a wish for contact; from a boss, pressure following you home; from someone you have lost, a deeply felt sense of connection that many people find comforting. Calls you cannot answer, or that ring and ring, can point to something asking for your attention. Sometimes a real sound, an alarm or a phone in the room, is woven into the dream. Notice whether you picked up and how the conversation felt.

contexts.when: A call from someone who has died
contexts.reading: Often vivid and consoling; many dreamers treasure these as a sense of continuing bond, whatever they believe about them.

contexts.when: It rings but you do not answer
contexts.reading: Something seeking your attention that you are avoiding, or not ready to hear.

contexts.when: You call someone and they answer warmly
contexts.reading: A wish for reconnection, or reassurance that a bond is still there.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the call as a wish to be reached by, or to reach, a particular person, the conversation standing in for words unsaid.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the caller may be a part of you sending a message from the unconscious; the dream asks whether you will pick up.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a verbal activity, with the phone as a communication object; a warm exchange may also be coded as friendliness.
lenses.modern: Outside sounds are often incorporated into dreams, so a ringing phone may come from the room; by continuity, calls echo who is on your mind.

reflect: Who was trying to reach me, and why?
Did I answer, and what was said?
Whom would I like to call right now?

name: Phone Not Working
summary: A phone that will not work is a common frustration dream: you need to reach someone urgently, but the call will not go through.
meaning: The keypad scrambles, the screen cracks, the numbers will not stay in order, or the call connects to silence. This classic dream mixes urgency with helplessness. It often mirrors a waking difficulty communicating: a conversation that keeps going wrong, a person who seems unreachable, or a fear that help will not come when needed. Notice whom you were trying to call and why. The purpose of the call, a warning, an apology, a request for help, often names what feels blocked.

contexts.when: Calling for help in an emergency
contexts.reading: Fear of being unsupported in a crisis; ask whom you would truly turn to, and whether they know.
A familiar dream effect; it can mirror confusion, or a message that refuses to take shape.
Relief and reconnection; a sign that communication may be easier than you fear.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask whether part of the dreamer does not want the call to connect, the broken phone protecting against a feared conversation.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the failed call may show a gap between the ego and another part of the psyche that has something to say.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a misfortune, an obstacle that befalls the dreamer; the phone is coded as a communication object.
lenses.modern: Fine detail such as digits on a keypad is often unstable in dreams, which may explain why these scenes are common; continuity links them to waking strain.

reflect: Whom am I struggling to reach right now?
What did I urgently need to say?
What would help that message get through?

name: Photograph
summary: A photograph holds memory: a fixed moment from the past, often carrying longing, comparison or a question about who you were.
meaning: Photographs in dreams often open onto people and periods that matter, especially ones that have ended. The feeling is usually the way in: warm nostalgia, an ache, or the strangeness of seeing yourself as you once were. Details can shift as you look, a face changing or a background you do not remember, which may show memory being reworked rather than simply recalled. A torn or faded photo can echo worry about losing a connection or forgetting a loved face.

contexts.reading: Often invites reflection on roots, belonging or a relationship you are revisiting in waking life.

contexts.when: The image changes as you look
contexts.reading: Can suggest that your understanding of the past is shifting, or that a memory is being reframed.

contexts.when: A photo is torn, burned or lost
contexts.reading: May echo grief, an ending, or a wish to let one version of the past go.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask who is in the picture and who is missing, treating the photo as a condensation of several memories.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, faces in the photograph may represent earlier selves, or ancestral figures the psyche is calling to mind.
lenses.hvdc: Coded in the communication class of objects; the coding also records the emotions it stirs, such as sadness or happiness.
lenses.modern: Dreaming appears to help consolidate and reorganize emotional memories, and a photograph is a natural image for that work.

reflect: Who was in the photograph, and who was missing?
What did you feel as you looked at it?
Is there a part of your past you are seeing differently now?

name: Piano
summary: A piano is about harmony, discipline and emotional range: practice, performance, and the many keys of feeling you can sound.
meaning: Because a piano spans so many notes, it can stand for the full range of what you feel and can express. Playing fluently may mirror harmony in your life or pride in a skill earned through practice. Freezing at a recital is a classic performance-anxiety image, often tied to evaluation by day. Keys that stick or sound wrong can echo something out of tune in a relationship or routine. A piano in a family home may bring back lessons, a parent's expectations, or music once shared.

contexts.reading: Often reflects harmony, mastery or emotional openness.
May echo fear of being judged or not being good enough.

contexts.when: The keys are wrong or silent
contexts.reading: Can mirror something in your life that feels out of tune.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might trace the piano to childhood lessons and to the people whose approval the playing sought.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, black and white keys working together can picture the union of opposites within the psyche.
lenses.hvdc: A piano is coded as an object, here with recreational implements; a failed performance can be coded as a failure.
lenses.modern: Practiced motor skills like playing an instrument can reappear in sleep, and performance stress carries over readily.

reflect: What were you playing, and for whom?
Did the music come easily?
What in your life feels in tune, or out of tune?

name: Pig
summary: The pig is commonly linked with appetite, indulgence and earthy pleasure, and also with abundance, good luck and intelligence.
meaning: Pigs carry a mixed reputation: greedy and dirty in insults, clever and lucky elsewhere (the pig signals wealth in Chinese tradition, and in German to 'have pig' means to be lucky). Dream pigs often raise questions about appetite and pleasure: eating, spending, comfort, desire. A pig rolling happily in mud can feel like permission to enjoy yourself. A greedy or filthy pig may reflect guilt or judgement about indulgence. A wild boar turns the image toward ferocity.

contexts.reading: Earthy enjoyment, or a need to stop judging simple pleasures.

contexts.when: A greedy pig at the trough
contexts.reading: Feelings about excess, your own or someone else's.
Raw, defensive aggression, or a temper that erupts.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the pig as appetite freed from manners: oral pleasure or desire the dreamer was taught to call dirty.
lenses.jung: In Jungian amplification the pig is linked with earth goddesses and fertility; as shadow, it carries the appetites the persona disowns.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; a boar's charge is coded as aggression, while pigs on a farm usually involve no interaction.
lenses.modern: Pig dreams often track waking concerns about eating, money or self-discipline, consistent with the continuity hypothesis.

reflect: How do I feel about my appetites right now?
Where do I judge myself for enjoying something?
Is there an area of excess I want to look at?

name: Pillow
summary: A pillow speaks of rest, comfort and private feeling: where you lay your head, your dreams, and what you confide to the dark.
meaning: A pillow is where thoughts settle at night, so in dreams it often relates to rest, privacy and the emotions you hold until you are alone. A soft pillow may mirror the comfort or ease you need; a hard or missing one can echo restlessness or a lack of support. Crying into a pillow may reflect feelings kept private. Something hidden under the pillow can carry a wish or a secret. A pillow fight brings back play and lightness, often with people from your past.

contexts.reading: Often reflects a need for rest and ease.
May mirror a secret wish, a worry or a hope kept close.
Can bring back playfulness, sibling ties or childhood joy.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask what you whisper or hide at the pillow, the most private place at the day's end.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the pillow sits at the border of sleep, where the ego lets go and the unconscious begins to speak.
lenses.hvdc: A pillow is coded as a household object.
lenses.modern: Sleep quality and comfort can shape dream content, and the pillow sometimes appears simply because the sleeper is half aware of it.

reflect: What did you rest, or hide, on the pillow?
How well have you been resting lately?
Which feelings do you keep for when you are alone?

name: Plane Crash
summary: A plane crash is a dramatic but common dream, especially around travel or big ambitions. It usually reflects fear of a plan or hope failing, not a forecast.
meaning: Planes carry us high and far, so a crash often speaks about ambitions, plans or expectations that feel as though they could come down: a launch at work, a move abroad, a relationship that took off quickly. People who fear flying, or have a trip coming up, may also dream of crashes simply as a rehearsal of that worry. Notice whether you were a passenger, the pilot or watching from the ground. Surviving, helping others or landing safely after all are common endings worth recording.

contexts.reading: Powerlessness in a situation someone else is steering; trust may be the real question.

contexts.when: You watch a plane come down
contexts.reading: Concern about someone else's ambitions, or about a public event you have been following.
Fear followed by safety: a sign you may cope better than you expect if plans change.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see an ambitious or forbidden wish soaring and then punished, the fall serving conscience as much as fear.
lenses.jung: Like Icarus, the crash may compensate for an attitude that has flown too high; on the subjective level, an inflated hope comes back to earth.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a misfortune, a bodily one if harm occurs; the plane is coded as a travel object.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, crash dreams often follow upcoming trips or news coverage; threat simulation theory sees them as rehearsal of a rare danger.

reflect: What plan or hope feels as though it could come down?
Was I a passenger, the pilot or a witness?
What would a safe landing look like for me now?

name: Playground
summary: A playground is the world of childhood play, often read as freedom, spontaneity and early social life, with its joys and its hurts.
meaning: Playgrounds take you back to swings, games and first friendships. Dreaming of one may reflect a longing for play and lightness, or the need to make room for spontaneity in a serious life. The same setting can recall early social pressures: being left out, teased or picked last. An empty playground can feel nostalgic or eerie. Watching children play may mirror tenderness for your younger self, or for children in your care.

contexts.reading: You may be reconnecting with joy, curiosity or lightness.
Old feelings of exclusion may be stirred by something happening now.
You may be missing a freer, earlier part of life.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading would look for childhood memories and wishes, and for early rivalries replayed in play.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the child archetype here: the playful, renewing part of the psyche that points toward the future.
lenses.hvdc: A playground is coded as an outdoor setting; children who appear are given the child age code.
lenses.modern: Childhood settings in adult dreams may draw on early memories when present emotions resemble them.

reflect: How old did you feel?
Who were you playing with?
Where could you make room for play in your life?

name: Playing a Game
summary: Playing a game is a widely shared dream of play, strategy and rules: a space where you can try things out with lower stakes.
meaning: Games in dreams can be pure fun, a return to the freedom of childhood play, or a picture of how you are handling the rules and moves of waking life. A board game may mirror strategy and patience; a team game, cooperation and belonging; a video game, challenges, levels and restarts. Notice whether you knew the rules, who you played with and how seriously you took it. Playfulness belongs to the book's Expansion pattern, and a dream that lets you play may be pointing to a need for more of it.

contexts.reading: Connection and lightness; you may be ready for more fun or collaboration in your life.

contexts.when: You do not know the rules
contexts.reading: Feeling new to a situation where others seem to know how it works; asking questions may help.
A sense of unfairness, or distrust of a person or situation; notice who it was.

lenses.freud: Freud saw children's play as creative wish fulfilment, rearranging the world to suit them; a dream game can do the same for the adult.
lenses.jung: Jung valued play and creative fantasy, recalling that as an adult he returned to childhood building games when he felt stuck.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an activity; cooperative play may be coded as a friendly interaction, and outcomes as success or failure.
lenses.modern: Games reappear readily in sleep; Stickgold and colleagues (2000) found that people who played Tetris often saw its falling shapes as they drifted off.

reflect: Where in my life could I be more playful?
Did I know the rules, and who made them?
Who was I playing with?

name: Police
summary: Police in a dream often represent rules, conscience and protection, and the fear or relief of being caught, judged or kept safe.
meaning: Police figures carry authority that can feel protective or threatening. When they help you, the dream may reflect a wish for order, rescue or support with something that feels out of control. When they pursue, question or arrest you, they may stand for guilt, self-criticism or worry about having broken a rule, even a small personal one. Sometimes you know you are innocent and still feel accused, which can echo being misunderstood in waking life. Notice which side of the law you feel on, and whose rules are being enforced.

contexts.reading: Often a wish for structure and safety, or trust that a problem can be put right.
This may reflect guilt or fear of consequences; ask whose rules you feel you have broken.
It can echo feeling misjudged, or an inner critic harsher than the facts.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the police as conscience in uniform, the inner authority Freud later called the superego, watching for forbidden wishes.
lenses.jung: Jung might read the police as a compensating force for order; on the subjective level, the part of you that patrols your boundaries.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as occupational characters, often a group; chasing or arresting the dreamer is coded as aggression, with the police as initiators.
lenses.modern: Dreams of being pursued by authority often rise with stress about deadlines, rules or mistakes, consistent with threat simulation views.

reflect: Which side of the law were you on?
Is there something you feel guilty about, fairly or not?
Whose rules are you trying to follow right now?

name: Potion
summary: A potion is transformation in liquid form: the hope of change, healing or power, and the risk of taking in something unknown.
meaning: Potions promise to change you from the inside, for better or worse, so their dreams often concern transformation and trust. Brewing one can mirror a creative process, combining the ingredients of your life into something new. Being offered a potion may echo an opportunity or influence you are unsure whether to accept. A love potion can reflect a wish to be wanted, or worry about manipulation. A potion that works may point to a change already underway inside you.

contexts.reading: Often reflects creativity, experimentation or inner change.
May echo an opportunity or influence you are weighing.
Can mirror transformation, or a shift you feel beginning.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the potion as a wish fulfilled by magic: to be loved, healed or powerful without the struggle.
lenses.jung: Jung saw the alchemists' elixir as an image of psychological transformation, the goal of the inner work he called individuation.
lenses.hvdc: A potion is coded as an object, usually in the miscellaneous class.
lenses.modern: Fantasy stories feed potion imagery into dreams, often as a picture of hoping for change, or fearing it.

reflect: What was the potion meant to do?
Did you drink it, and how did you feel?
What change are you hoping for, or wary of?

name: Praying
summary: Praying is a widely shared dream of reaching toward something larger: asking for help, giving thanks or seeking peace.
meaning: Prayer dreams come to people of every faith and of none. For the religious, they may continue a real practice and carry its comfort; for others, the act may express a longing for guidance, forgiveness or a sense of not being alone. The content of the prayer is often the heart of the dream: what you asked for, for whom, and whether you felt heard. Notice the setting too. A familiar place of worship, a childhood bedside or an open field each suggest a different relationship with the sacred.

contexts.reading: Care and concern; the dream may show how much that person is on your mind.
Peace, reassurance or a sense of being held; notice how it felt in the body.
A need you cannot yet name; writing it down in waking life may help.

lenses.freud: Freud read religious feeling in terms of longing for a protective parent; a Freudian reading might ask whose protection the dreamer seeks.
lenses.jung: Jung took religious experience seriously as the psyche's relation to the Self; prayer may be a dialogue with that wider centre.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a verbal or thinking activity; the religious setting and objects are recorded among settings and objects.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, prayer dreams often reflect waking spiritual practice or periods of worry; they may carry calm into the morning.

reflect: What was I asking for, and for whom?
Did I feel heard?
Where do I find a sense of support beyond myself?

name: Pregnancy
summary: Pregnancy in a dream usually symbolises creation and growth: something developing in your life that is not yet ready to be born.
meaning: Dreams of being pregnant, or of someone else being pregnant, are often about gestation: an idea, a project, a relationship or a new version of yourself taking shape. They can feel joyful, anxious or simply strange, and they come to people of any gender and any age. Excitement may reflect anticipation of change; fear may point to doubts about readiness or responsibility. Such dreams do not mean you are pregnant. If pregnancy is part of your waking life, the dream may simply be processing that experience, with its hopes and its worries.

contexts.reading: Often anticipation of something new you are nurturing.

contexts.when: The pregnancy feels frightening or wrong
contexts.reading: This may reflect doubts about readiness, or pressure to produce something too soon.
You may be noticing growth in them, or a quality of theirs developing in you.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see wishes about creation, continuation or being cared for, alongside fears about responsibility.
lenses.jung: Jung might see a new attitude or a new aspect of the Self forming in the unconscious, not yet ready for daylight.
lenses.hvdc: There is no code for pregnancy itself; the coder records the characters, the emotions and, where mentioned, torso and anatomy body parts.
lenses.modern: During a real pregnancy, dreams often turn to the coming baby and the changing body, consistent with the continuity hypothesis.

reflect: What is growing in your life right now?
How ready do you feel for it?
What does it need from you while it develops?

name: Prison
summary: A prison is confinement, often read as feeling restricted by circumstances, obligations or your own guilt and self-judgement.
meaning: Prison dreams usually say more about freedom than about crime. Being locked up may mirror a job, relationship, routine or belief that feels confining, or a weight of guilt you keep carrying. Notice who holds the keys. Sometimes the cell door stands open and you stay, which can point to limits that have simply become familiar. Visiting someone in prison may reflect concern for a person who seems stuck. Escaping or being released often comes with a growing sense of freedom.

contexts.reading: Something in your life may feel confining; ask what the walls are made of.

contexts.when: The door is open, but you stay
contexts.reading: A limit may be more habit than necessity.
You may be moving toward freedom from an old restriction.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the prison as conscience at work, punishing a forbidden wish the dreamer may not admit.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading would ask which part of the psyche is imprisoned, perhaps a shadow quality or a creative energy denied expression.
lenses.hvdc: Prisons are architecture objects in an indoor setting, coded familiar only if you know the place.
lenses.modern: Confinement dreams may reflect waking stress about autonomy; in threat-simulation terms, they may rehearse escape.

reflect: What were you held for, if you knew?
Who held the keys?
Which restriction in your life might you loosen?

name: Public Speaking
summary: Speaking in front of a crowd is a common dream of exposure and voice: having to explain yourself, persuade or simply be heard.
meaning: The microphone squeals, the notes are in a language you cannot read, or every face in the hall is someone you know. Public speaking dreams concentrate a familiar fear: that your words will fail you when it counts. Yet some people dream of speaking brilliantly, the room hanging on every word, which can reflect growing confidence or a message you are ready to share. Notice what you were trying to say and who was listening. That message, even half-remembered, may be something you need to say awake.

contexts.reading: Pressure and self-doubt; it often appears before real presentations or conversations that matter.
May reflect feeling unheard at work or at home, or doubt that your view carries weight.

contexts.when: You speak with ease and power
contexts.reading: Confidence emerging, or permission to claim your voice in a situation that needs it.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might look at what the speech conceals as much as what it says, and at a wish for admiration hidden behind the fear.
lenses.jung: The speaker stands where persona meets the collective; the dream may ask whether you speak in your own voice or a borrowed one.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a verbal activity; the audience is coded as a group character, and its reactions as friendly or aggressive interactions.
lenses.modern: Social threat is a common dream theme; by the continuity hypothesis, such dreams may cluster before real talks, interviews and difficult conversations.

reflect: What do I need to say that I have not said?
Who was in the audience?
Did my voice feel like my own?

name: Puppy
summary: A puppy is widely read as new beginnings, playful affection and innocence, something young that needs care and training.
meaning: A puppy brings energy, clumsy affection and complete trust, so dream puppies often arrive with new beginnings: a relationship, a project, a fresh start that needs attention and patience. Caring for one may mirror your own nurturing side, or responsibilities you have taken on. A puppy that misbehaves can reflect an enthusiastic but untrained part of you. A lost or hurt puppy often stirs protectiveness, perhaps toward someone else, perhaps toward your own younger self.

contexts.reading: Joy, affection and a lighter mood.
A new responsibility or beginning that needs patience.
A vulnerable part of you, or of someone close, that needs protecting.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the puppy as a wish for unconditional love, or as a displaced image of a baby or younger sibling.
lenses.jung: In Jungian terms the puppy can carry the child archetype in animal form: new life, potential and vulnerability.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; playing with or cuddling it is coded as friendliness between the dreamer and the puppy.
lenses.modern: Puppy dreams often follow a new pet, a birth or a fresh start, and usually carry positive emotion, as continuity would expect.

reflect: What new beginning needs my patience?
What playful part of me wants more room?
Who in my life needs gentle protection?

name: Queen
summary: A queen often represents dignity, influence and feminine authority: power held with grace, or with coldness.
meaning: A queen in a dream may stand for a powerful woman in your life, often a mother figure, or for leadership, poise and self-respect in yourself, whatever your gender. A gracious queen can reflect confidence and composure; a cold or cruel one may echo a controlling presence, perfectionism or a fear of judgement. Being crowned yourself can point to stepping into your worth or into a new role. A queen alone on her throne may also speak of the loneliness that sometimes comes with responsibility. The feeling she leaves you with is the best guide.

contexts.reading: Often self-respect and composure, or a model of leadership you are drawing on.
This may echo a controlling figure, or your own demands for perfection.
This can reflect claiming your worth or authority, and the responsibility that comes with it.

lenses.freud: Freud linked queens and empresses in dreams to the dreamer's mother, and princesses to the dreamer; a Freudian reading begins with the mother.
lenses.jung: Jung saw the royal pair as an image of the union of opposites; a queen alone can carry the great mother, generous or devouring.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a female adult character; like other famous or powerful figures, a real queen is coded with the prominent identity.
lenses.modern: Dreams of royalty often follow questions of status, respect and influence, and may reflect how you see your own authority.

reflect: How did the queen treat you?
Where do you need more self-respect right now?
What would graceful authority look like for you?

name: Rabbit
summary: Rabbits and hares are widely linked with fertility, abundance, gentleness and quickness, and also with timidity and the urge to flee.
meaning: Rabbits multiply quickly and live in constant alertness, so they gather two meanings: abundance and new beginnings, and nervousness, the freeze before flight. A soft rabbit in your arms may reflect tenderness, or a gentle part of you that wants care. A rabbit bolting away may mirror an impulse to run from something. Following a white rabbit, as Alice does, often signals curiosity leading you into unfamiliar territory: a new idea, or a strange season of life.

contexts.reading: Tenderness, vulnerability, and a part of you that needs gentle care.
An urge to flee, or a moment of nervous paralysis before a decision.

contexts.when: You follow it down a hole
contexts.reading: Curiosity drawing you into the unknown; notice whether it feels exciting or disorienting.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might link the rabbit's fertility to wishes or worries about sexuality or having children, softened into a harmless form.
lenses.jung: The hare is a trickster in many folk tales and the moon hare of East Asian myth; a Jungian reading weighs both its cleverness and its vulnerability.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; holding or stroking it is coded as friendliness from the dreamer toward the animal.
lenses.modern: Rabbit dreams often accompany jittery periods; the freeze or flee behaviour may mirror how your body has been reacting to waking stress.

reflect: Where do I want to run, and where do I freeze?
What new beginning is multiplying in my life?
What curiosity might be leading me somewhere new?

name: Rat
summary: Rats are commonly read as anxiety, contamination or betrayal, something gnawing in the background, and also as survival and resourcefulness.
meaning: Rats thrive where people would rather not look: under floors, in waste, behind walls. In dreams they often carry what gnaws at you quietly, a worry, a guilty feeling, a suspicion that someone is not loyal. Many rats can reflect anxiety that has multiplied. Yet rats are survivors, clever and adaptable, and some dreamers find them neutral or even endearing, especially if they have kept them as pets. Your own reaction matters most.

contexts.reading: Worries or resentments moving just out of sight.
A betrayal, or a nagging problem that finally demands attention.

contexts.when: A pet rat, or a calm one
contexts.reading: Resourcefulness and survival instinct, a part of you that copes in hard places.

lenses.freud: Freud linked small animals and vermin with small children, often unwanted siblings; his 'Rat Man' case (1909) also shows one rat image condensing several meanings.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading sees the rat as a shadow figure: what lives in the basement of the psyche, disowned but clever and hard to get rid of.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character, a mass of rats as a group; a bite is physical aggression toward the dreamer.
lenses.modern: Rat dreams often follow waking stress about mess, money or trust; the gnawing quality mirrors how an unaddressed worry feels.

reflect: What is gnawing at me quietly right now?
Do I doubt someone's loyalty, or my own?
Where might I be more resourceful than I give myself credit for?

name: Reading
summary: Reading in dreams is about seeking knowledge or a message: taking in words that may explain, instruct or reveal something you need.
meaning: Dreamers often remember the act of reading more clearly than the words themselves. A book can stand for knowledge, a story you are living or wisdom you are reaching for; a letter, news or a message from someone in particular. Many dreamers notice that dream text blurs, rearranges or turns to nonsense on a second look, a quirk of the dreaming brain rather than a failing of yours. Notice what you were trying to learn. A page you could finally read, or a single sentence you remember, can be worth carrying into the day.

contexts.reading: Curiosity and openness; you may be ready to learn or understand something new.

contexts.when: The words will not stay still
contexts.reading: A familiar dream effect; if you notice it, you may be close to realising you are dreaming.

contexts.when: Reading a letter meant for you
contexts.reading: A message you are waiting for, or one you need to hear from yourself.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might treat any words recalled from the page as condensed messages, worth free association for what they bring to mind.
lenses.jung: Reading can be a search for meaning in the collective store of wisdom; on the subjective level, the book may be your own unfolding story.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a visual activity, with the book or letter coded as a communication object.
lenses.modern: Stephen LaBerge's lucid dreaming work recommends rereading text as a reality check, since dream text rarely stays the same twice.

reflect: What was I trying to learn or understand?
Did any words stay with me after waking?
Who might the message have been from?

name: Realising You Are Dreaming
summary: Realising you are dreaming while the dream goes on is lucid dreaming, a widely reported experience described from ancient times to modern sleep laboratories.
meaning: Something odd catches your attention, and suddenly you know: this is a dream. The moment often brings exhilaration and clarity, and some dreamers then fly, explore or ask the dream questions. Lucidity can also be fragile; excitement may wake you, or the dream may pull you back into its plot. It fits the book's Expansion pattern well: curiosity, openness, a new relationship with your own inner world. Many people find that keeping a journal and noticing recurring dream signs makes lucid moments more frequent.

contexts.reading: A sense of freedom and agency; notice what you chose to do with it.
Common at first; staying calm and focusing on the dream's details can help it last.
Some dreamers use lucidity to face a fear or seek insight; the answer may come as an image.

lenses.freud: Freud noted that the thought 'it is only a dream' can arise within a dream, and read it as a way of making a disturbing scene bearable so that sleep can go on.
lenses.jung: Lucidity can resemble Jung's active imagination, a conscious dialogue with images from the unconscious, here taking place inside the dream itself.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a thinking activity of the dreamer; the coding records lucidity's effects, such as flying or emotions, rather than lucidity itself.
lenses.modern: LaBerge's laboratory work showed lucid dreamers signalling with planned eye movements during REM sleep; Voss and colleagues (2009) found more frontal brain activity in lucid dreams.

reflect: What made me realise I was dreaming?
What did I choose to do once I knew?
What would I like to explore next time?

name: Receiving a Gift
summary: Receiving a gift is a widely shared dream of being valued: something offered to you, often carrying a message about what you need or are ready to accept.
meaning: Dream gifts can be ordinary or magical: a book, a ring, a key, a box that holds something unexpected. What is inside often speaks of a quality or opportunity arriving in your life, or one you wish would arrive. Who gives it matters as much. A gift from someone you have lost can bring comfort; from a stranger, a sense of unexpected help; from a rival, a softening of tension. Notice how you felt receiving it. Ease suggests openness; awkwardness may point to difficulty accepting care or praise.

contexts.when: A gift from someone who has died
contexts.reading: Often deeply comforting; many dreamers feel it as love or reassurance carried forward.
Expectations not met, or a hope that has not yet taken shape.
Something offered to you that you are not yet ready, or able, to receive.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading treats the gift as a wish fulfilled, the giver often a stand-in for someone whose love or approval is longed for.
lenses.jung: In myth and fairy tale, gifts from helpers mark a turning point on the hero's path; the gift may symbolise a new capacity arriving from the unconscious.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a friendly interaction with the dreamer as recipient; the gift is coded as an object.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, gift dreams may echo real occasions or a longing for recognition; they often leave a warm mood on waking.

reflect: What was the gift, and what might it represent?
Who gave it to me?
How easily do I accept what others offer?

name: Rejection
summary: Rejection in a dream often reflects a fear of not being accepted or not being enough, and the sting of past or present hurts.
meaning: Being turned down, dumped, excluded or refused in a dream can feel as raw as the real thing. These dreams often surface before something where acceptance matters: an application, a new relationship, a social event. They can also replay old rejections that still ache, especially when a present situation touches the same nerve. The dream may be giving the fear a safe rehearsal. Notice who rejects you and how you respond. Recovering, walking away with dignity or finding acceptance elsewhere in the dream can mirror growing resilience.

contexts.reading: Often a fear of not being wanted; it says more about your doubts than your worth.

contexts.when: Rejected by a group or at work
contexts.reading: This may reflect worry about belonging, standing or being good enough.
This can show boundaries forming, or a part of you being pushed away.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might trace the sting back to early experiences of a parent's attention going elsewhere, such as to a sibling.
lenses.jung: Jung might ask what the rejecting figure represents; sometimes we reject in others what we have not accepted in ourselves.
lenses.hvdc: Rejection can be coded as a non-physical form of aggression toward the dreamer, and the hurt as sadness or apprehension.
lenses.modern: Threat and social simulation views both suggest dreams rehearse social threats such as exclusion, which may help prepare for them.

reflect: Who rejected you, and how did it feel?
When have you felt this before?
What would self-acceptance look like here?

name: Rescuing Someone
aliases: pulling someone out of the water
summary: Rescuing someone is a widely shared dream of courage and care: reaching into danger to bring another person, or a creature, to safety.
meaning: You dive into the river, carry a child from a burning house, pull a friend back from an edge. Rescue dreams often feel urgent and meaningful, and they usually mirror care and responsibility: for family, friends, colleagues or people you feel you should protect. Who you save matters. A loved one points to concern for them; a stranger or an animal may stand for a vulnerable part of yourself. Notice how it ended. Success can reflect confidence in your capacity to help; failure, the weight of responsibilities that are not all yours to carry.

contexts.reading: Care and concern, often heightened by worry; love speaking as protection, not prediction.

contexts.when: Saving a stranger or an animal
contexts.reading: Compassion, or a vulnerable part of you calling for attention.

contexts.when: You cannot reach them in time
contexts.reading: Responsibility that feels too heavy; ask what is truly yours to carry, and what is not.

lenses.freud: Freud connected dreams of rescuing someone, especially from water, with the theme of birth; a Freudian reading also asks whom the dreamer longs to protect.
lenses.jung: Rescuing is the hero archetype at work; on the subjective level, the one you save may be your own neglected or endangered side.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a friendly interaction with the dreamer as befriender; a successful rescue through effort can also be scored as a success.
lenses.modern: Threat simulation theory sees protective action as rehearsal; by the continuity hypothesis, rescue dreams often echo caring roles in waking life.

reflect: Whom was I rescuing, and from what?
Who might I be trying to protect in waking life?
What part of me needs rescuing?

name: Restaurant
summary: A restaurant is nourishment served by others, often read as how you receive care, pleasure and choice, and who you share them with.
meaning: Unlike a kitchen, a restaurant feeds you without asking you to cook. Dreams set in one often concern receiving: enjoying pleasure, being served, choosing from a menu of options. A relaxed meal with friends may mirror satisfaction and connection. Long waits, wrong orders or a bill you cannot pay can echo frustration that your needs go unmet, or worry about what pleasure costs. Being the server rather than the guest may reflect a habit of caring for others first.

contexts.reading: You may be appreciating connection, celebration or a period of ease.

contexts.when: Waiting forever, or served the wrong dish
contexts.reading: Your needs may feel overlooked or misunderstood.
You may be giving more care than you receive.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might trace appetite back to early oral satisfaction, and look at who feeds whom.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the shared meal as a communion, inner figures gathering at one table.
lenses.hvdc: Restaurants are architecture objects in an indoor setting; the food is coded in the food class.
lenses.modern: Eating out in dreams often reflects social life and daily routine, consistent with continuity with waking experience.

reflect: Who were you eating with?
Did you get what you ordered?
Where in life are you being well served, or not?

name: Reunion
summary: A reunion is a widely shared dream of reconnection: meeting again someone from the past, often with warmth, longing or unfinished feelings.
meaning: An old friend at a station, a sibling you rarely see, a former classmate, sometimes someone who has died: reunion dreams bring people back. Often they feel tender, a sense of being known again by someone who remembers who you were. They can also stir questions: what changed, what was left unsaid, why this person now. Notice the setting and the feeling in the embrace. Joy suggests a bond still alive in you; awkwardness, distance or change; tears, a longing or grief being touched. Reunions with the deceased can be especially comforting.

contexts.when: A joyful reunion with an old friend
contexts.reading: A part of your past, or of yourself, you may want to reconnect with.

contexts.when: Reunited with someone who has died
contexts.reading: Often deeply comforting; many dreamers describe a sense of continuing bond.
Unfinished business or change; what would you say if you met again for real?

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the reunion as a wish fulfilled, bringing back someone the dreamer longs for, with day residue choosing the moment.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the returning figure may carry a quality you once had and are now reclaiming; reunion can picture inner integration.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a friendly interaction, with characters coded by identity (family, known, dead or imaginary) and emotion recorded as felt.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, reunion dreams may follow anniversaries, old photos or news of someone; they often carry strong positive emotion.

reflect: Who came back into my dream, and why now?
What did the reunion feel like?
Is there someone I would like to reconnect with?

name: Ring
summary: A ring stands for commitment and wholeness: a bond, a promise, or a sense of completeness that circles back on itself.
meaning: Because a ring has no beginning or end, it carries ideas of continuity and promise. Being given a ring can mirror a deepening bond or a commitment you are ready to make, whether to a person, a path or yourself. Losing one often echoes worry about a relationship or a vow, though it may also point to a commitment that no longer fits. A ring that is too tight or will not come off can speak of obligation more than love.

contexts.reading: May reflect commitment, belonging or recognition, in love or in other parts of life.
Often echoes fear for a bond, or a question about whether a promise still fits.

contexts.when: It is too tight, or stuck
contexts.reading: Can mirror a commitment that has begun to feel binding rather than chosen.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might focus on what the ring promises or forbids, and on the person who gave it.
lenses.jung: Jung saw the ring and the circle as images of wholeness and of the Self; a ring can also mark the union of inner opposites.
lenses.hvdc: A ring is coded as an object, most likely with clothing and adornment; receiving one can be coded as a friendly interaction.
lenses.modern: Rings often surface around real commitments, anniversaries or separations, as the mind processes the emotion attached to them.

reflect: Who gave you the ring, or whom were you giving it to?
Did it fit comfortably?
Which promise in your life is on your mind?

name: Road
summary: The road is one of the oldest images of a life's direction: where you are heading, how the journey feels and what lies ahead.
meaning: A road suggests movement with purpose, and its condition often mirrors how your direction in life feels. A smooth, open road may reflect confidence and momentum; potholes, fog or roadworks, delays and uncertainty. Winding roads suggest a slow or unpredictable route; a dead end, a plan that may need rethinking. Notice whether you chose the road, how you travelled it, on foot or by car, and whether anyone was with you. Being on the road alone can feel free or lonely.

contexts.reading: You may feel sure of your direction and free to move.

contexts.when: Blocked, flooded or a dead end
contexts.reading: A plan may be stalled; another route may exist.

contexts.when: No signs, no idea where you are
contexts.reading: You may be unsure where a choice will lead.

lenses.freud: Freud noted that setting out on a journey can stand for life's great departures; a Freudian reading also asks where, and toward whom, the road leads.
lenses.jung: The road is a classic image of the individuation journey; a Jungian reading looks at companions, obstacles and turnings along the way.
lenses.hvdc: Roads belong to the streets class of objects, and scenes on them are outdoor settings.
lenses.modern: Journey dreams may reflect waking concerns about direction and progress, consistent with the continuity hypothesis.

reflect: Where was the road taking you, and did you want to go?
What was the road like under you?
Which direction in your life is this road about?

name: Robot
summary: A robot raises questions about what is mechanical and what is human: routine, control, emotion switched off, and the fear or promise of new technology.
meaning: Robots in dreams often reflect how human you feel in your own life. Moving like a robot, or being one, can mirror running on autopilot, numbness, or a routine that has drained the feeling from your days. A helpful robot may echo trust in technology or a wish for support with heavy tasks. A robot that turns against people often carries anxieties about control, replacement or change. Talking with an artificial mind, now a waking experience for many, can become a way of talking with yourself.

contexts.reading: Often reflects autopilot, emotional distance or an exhausting routine.
May mirror a wish for support, efficiency or relief.
Can echo fears about control, being replaced or rapid change.

lenses.freud: Freud's essay on the uncanny (1919) explored the unease of figures that may or may not be alive, which robots evoke strongly.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, a robot can picture a function cut off from feeling: the ego working without soul, asking to be reconnected.
lenses.hvdc: A robot that acts or speaks is coded as a character, usually among imaginary figures; one that only stands is an object in the implements class.
lenses.modern: News and daily use of technology, including artificial intelligence, feed directly into dreams, a clear case of continuity.

reflect: Was the robot a friend, a threat, or you?
Where in your life are you running on autopilot?
What would bring more feeling back into your days?

name: Roof
summary: A roof is shelter overhead; standing on one is often read as reaching a high, exposed vantage point.
meaning: Two quite different dreams use this image. Under a roof, attention falls on protection: a sound roof may mirror feeling safe, while a leaking, collapsing or missing one may echo worry that your shelter, whether money, health, home or support, will not hold. On a roof, the feeling shifts to height and exposure. The view can be thrilling and the edge frightening. Climbing up may reflect ambition or escape; being stranded there, the sense of having gone further than feels safe.

contexts.reading: Something that protects you may feel strained; it could help to notice what needs repair.

contexts.when: Standing on top with a wide view
contexts.reading: You may be seeing your situation from a new height, with confidence or with nerves.
You may feel overextended, too far out to climb down easily.

lenses.freud: Since Freud accepted the house as an image of the body, a Freudian reading might link the roof with the head, and climbing onto it with daring wishes.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the rooftop as a height of consciousness, where perspective is gained but the ground of instinct feels far away.
lenses.hvdc: An architecture object; standing on a roof places the scene outdoors, while a leak seen from inside is an indoor setting.
lenses.modern: Heights readily trigger threat rehearsal in dreams; fear at the edge may mirror waking situations where the stakes feel high.

reflect: Were you under the roof or on top of it?
What feels like shelter in your life right now, and is it holding?
What could you see from up there?

name: Rope
summary: A rope can hold you up or hold you back: a lifeline, a tie that binds, or a connection under strain.
meaning: Rope is about connection and tension. Thrown to you, it can feel like help arriving or a relationship that holds; climbing one may mirror effort toward a goal with little to stand on. Being tied up often echoes obligations, guilt or a situation you feel unable to leave. Knots and tangles tend to reflect problems that need patience more than force. A fraying rope can speak of trust or support wearing thin, and is worth noticing early.

contexts.reading: May reflect support offered, or hope in a hard situation.
Often echoes feeling restricted by duty, a relationship or your own fears.
Can mirror worry that a support or connection will not hold.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask who holds the other end of the rope, and what early tie it repeats.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, a rope can be the link between conscious and unconscious, or between you and a guiding figure.
lenses.hvdc: Coded in the implements class; tying up a character is coded as physical aggression, and pulling someone to safety as friendliness.
lenses.modern: Dreams of being held or bound often accompany waking constraints, and rescue images may show the mind looking for support.

reflect: Was the rope helping you or holding you?
Who was on the other end?
Which connection in your life feels strong, or strained?

name: Ruins
summary: Ruins are what remains after time or upheaval, often read as the past, its lessons and the ground on which something new can be built.
meaning: Ruins hold two feelings at once: loss and endurance. Something fell, yet something remains. Dreaming of them may reflect an ending, a relationship, a plan or an earlier self, that you are still walking through. Ancient ruins often carry wonder, a sense of long history and of what outlasts us. The recent ruin of a familiar place may feel more raw. Exploring calmly can show readiness to learn from the past; rebuilding among the stones, that renewal has begun.

contexts.reading: You may be discovering roots, history or a perspective larger than daily concerns.

contexts.when: Your own home or town in ruins
contexts.reading: An important part of life may feel broken, or changed beyond recognition.
You may be beginning again with what survived.

lenses.freud: Freud often compared psychoanalysis to archaeology; a Freudian reading of ruins digs toward buried memories beneath the present.
lenses.jung: In Jung's house dream the deepest levels held ancient remains; a Jungian reading treats ruins as traces of personal and collective history.
lenses.hvdc: Ruins are architecture objects, usually in an outdoor setting, coded geographical when they are a named real site you have not visited.
lenses.modern: Dreams of loss and decay may help integrate change, consistent with accounts of emotional processing during REM sleep.

reflect: What were these ruins once, and what is left?
Which ending in your life are you still walking through?
What could be built from what remains?

name: Running
summary: Running in dreams usually carries urgency or drive: racing toward a goal, away from a threat, or simply moving through life at speed.
meaning: Running is one of the plainest pictures of how you are pacing yourself, and its direction and ease carry the meaning. Running freely, lungs full and legs strong, can reflect energy and momentum you have recently found. Running to catch something suggests a deadline or an opportunity; running with no clear destination may mirror restlessness or a schedule that never pauses. Over time, notice whether your dream running grows lighter or heavier: that change can mirror your waking reserves.

contexts.reading: A vivid sense of vitality; it often appears when you feel capable and unburdened, or when you miss that feeling.
A goal with a clock on it. Ask whether the pace is yours or set by others.

contexts.when: Running in circles or on the spot
contexts.reading: Effort without progress: a picture of routines that consume energy but do not move you forward.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask what the running hurries toward or away from, treating the destination as the disguised wish and the speed as its urgency.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, running can show the ego outpacing other parts of the psyche; compensation may ask you to slow down so they can arrive.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a movement activity of the dreamer; if a pursuer is present, the chase is coded separately as an aggressive interaction.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, dream running often reflects waking pace: busy, pressured periods can bring hurried movement into dreams.

reflect: Where in my life am I running, and toward what?
Did the running feel free or forced?
What would happen if I slowed to a walk?

name: Saying Goodbye
summary: Saying goodbye is a widely shared dream of endings and transitions: parting from a person, a place or a stage of life, often with tenderness.
meaning: Farewell dreams can hold great feeling: a long embrace at a station, a wave from a window, words you wish you had said. They often accompany real transitions, a move, a child growing up, the end of a job or relationship, and sometimes a death. In the book's terms, a goodbye can carry Descent and, in time, a quiet acceptance. Dreams of saying goodbye to someone who has died are often described as a gift, a chance to finish what was left open. Notice who left whom, and how it felt to watch them go.

contexts.reading: Acceptance and gratitude; you may be ready to let a chapter close.

contexts.when: A goodbye you could not say in life
contexts.reading: Many dreamers find comfort in this; it may help a grief to soften.

contexts.when: Unable to leave, or to let go
contexts.reading: Attachment to what is ending; what would help you take the next step?

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the farewell as a wish to resolve mixed feelings toward the one departing, giving them a final, gentler form.
lenses.jung: Goodbyes mark thresholds in individuation; on the subjective level, you may be parting from an old role or attitude.
lenses.hvdc: The farewell itself is a verbal activity; warmth shown, such as a hug, is coded as friendliness, and sorrow as sadness.
lenses.modern: Emotion processing views suggest dreams can help work through endings; by the continuity hypothesis, they often follow real partings.

reflect: What, or whom, am I saying goodbye to in my life?
What did I say, or wish I had said?
What helps me let go gently?

name: School
summary: School is one of the most widely reported dream settings, often returning long after school ends, when you feel tested, judged or still learning.
meaning: Many adults dream of school decades after leaving it. The setting tends to appear when waking life brings back what school taught us to feel: being evaluated, fitting in, being unprepared, competing, wanting approval. A lost locker, a missed class or an unreadable timetable often mirrors a current test at work or in relationships. Pleasant school dreams can recall curiosity and friendship. Notice your age in the dream, and whether you were a student, a teacher or a visitor.

contexts.when: Lost, late or cannot find your class
contexts.reading: You may feel unprepared, or unsure of what is expected of you now.
Questions of belonging, comparison or old friendship may be stirring.

contexts.when: Returning as an adult or a teacher
contexts.reading: You may be bringing what you have learned to a new situation.

lenses.freud: Freud discussed examination dreams, often about tests already passed, and read them as reassurance when a new responsibility looms.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading treats school as a place of learning and initiation, recurring when a new lesson of individuation is under way.
lenses.hvdc: School buildings are architecture objects; the scene is usually indoor and often familiar from your own past.
lenses.modern: Recurring school dreams long after school are widely reported; old settings may stand in for present evaluation, as the continuity hypothesis suggests.

reflect: Which school was it, and how old did you feel?
What were you supposed to know or do?
Where in your life do you feel tested right now?

name: Scissors
summary: Scissors are about cutting ties and shaping: separating, ending, trimming away excess, and making something new from what remains.
meaning: Unlike a knife, scissors are tools of precision and craft, so their dreams often concern deliberate separation. Cutting a cord or ribbon can mirror ending a relationship, a dependency or a chapter, sometimes with relief. Cutting paper or fabric may reflect shaping a project, editing your life to fit. Scissors in someone else's hands can echo worry about being cut off or cut down to size. Feeling uneasy around them may point to a separation you are not yet ready for.

contexts.when: You cut a cord or ribbon
contexts.reading: Often reflects ending a tie, a phase or a dependency.
May mirror shaping, editing or creating something new.
Can echo fear of being cut off, criticized or diminished.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might link cutting with fears of loss or punishment, and with separations the dreamer both wishes for and dreads.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, scissors can stand for discrimination: deciding consciously what to keep and what to cut away.
lenses.hvdc: Scissors are coded in the implements class; using them against a character is coded as aggression.
lenses.modern: Endings and separations in waking life, from moving out to breakups, often find expression in images of cutting.

reflect: What were you cutting, or trying to cut?
Was the cut a relief or a loss?
What in your life is ready to be trimmed away?

name: Scorpion
summary: The scorpion is widely read as hidden danger, defensiveness and the sting of hurt or betrayal, and also as fierce self-protection.
meaning: A scorpion is small but carries its weapon raised, so dreams often use it for danger from something you underestimated, or for a sharp, defensive reaction. Scorpion dreams can arise around hurtful words, jealousy or betrayal: a sting that lingers. They can also reflect your own armour, the part of you ready to strike back when threatened. Desert settings add a sense of harsh, dry conditions where only the tough get through.

contexts.reading: A painful remark, betrayal or consequence that lingers after the moment.

contexts.when: Hidden in your shoe or bed
contexts.reading: A threat in a place you expected to be safe; trust may feel shaken.
Your own defensiveness, or someone else's readiness to hurt.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the sting as displaced aggression: the dreamer's own wish to hurt, or a fear of punishment for it.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading may treat the scorpion as shadow: venom kept for self-protection that can turn on you or on those close to you.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; a sting is physical aggression, and your fear is coded as apprehension even if it never strikes.
lenses.modern: Scorpion dreams fit threat simulation (Revonsuo 2000) and often follow a conflict in which someone's words stung.

reflect: Whose words have stung me recently?
When do I raise my own tail in defence?
Where did I expect safety and find danger?

name: Seal
summary: Seals are often read as moving between worlds, land and sea, and as playfulness, curiosity and longing for home.
meaning: A seal is clumsy on land and graceful in water, so it can mirror feeling out of place in one part of life and at home in another. In Scottish and Irish folklore the selkie is a seal who becomes human and always longs to return to the sea, a story about belonging and identity. Dream seals often carry curiosity and gentleness, with dark eyes that seem to look right at you. A seal pup alone may stir protectiveness or vulnerability.

contexts.when: It watches you from the water
contexts.reading: Curiosity, gentle contact, or something from the depths looking back at you.

contexts.when: Clumsy on land, graceful in water
contexts.reading: Out of your element in one place, at ease in another.
Vulnerability, or an instinct to protect someone.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the selkie's longing for the sea as a wish to return to an earlier, freer state.
lenses.jung: Selkie tales support a Jungian reading of the seal as a soul figure moving between the land of consciousness and the sea of the unconscious.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; a seal approaching you is friendliness, and a beach or shore an outdoor setting.
lenses.modern: Seal dreams often draw on coastal memories or travel, and may carry questions about where you feel at home.

reflect: Where do I feel out of my element, and where at home?
What am I longing to return to?
What part of me needs protection right now?

name: Searching
summary: Searching is a widely shared dream of looking for something or someone just out of reach, often a picture of a need not yet met.
meaning: Searching dreams can feel endless: room after room, bag after bag, street after street. What you seek is the first clue, and it is not always literal. A missing key can stand for access or a solution, a lost person for a connection you miss, an unnamed something for a direction you have not found. The feeling matters as much as the object. Anxious searching suggests pressure to fix something quickly, while curious searching belongs to Expansion: exploring, opening doors, finding parts of a place you did not know existed.

contexts.reading: Can mirror a longing still unmet, or a sense that you are looking in the wrong place; ask where else it could be.
A familiar dream twist: what you needed may differ from what you thought you wanted.
Exploration more than loss; often a sign of openness to new interests, places or ideas.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading treats the sought object as a stand-in, displaced from the true wish, and invites free association to whatever it brings to mind.
lenses.jung: The search is a classic picture of individuation: the quest for something whole, which Jung called the Self, glimpsed through many symbolic objects.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a physical or visual activity; finding the object can be scored as a success when it comes through the dreamer's own effort.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, the search often borrows waking preoccupations: misplaced items, unanswered questions, unfinished tasks.

reflect: What am I really looking for at the moment?
Was I searching anxiously or with curiosity?
Where have I not looked yet, in the dream or in life?

name: Sewing
summary: Sewing is about mending and making: repairing what has torn, joining pieces together, and patient work that gives things new form.
meaning: Sewing joins what was separate and mends what was torn, so its dreams often concern relationships, healing and creativity.
