lenses.modern: Travel plans and deadlines often appear in dreams in the days before a trip, a clear case of continuity.

reflect: Where was the ticket meant to take you?
Did you feel you had the right to go?
What opportunity are you waiting for permission to take?

name: Tiger
summary: The tiger is often read as raw power, passion and intensity: beauty and danger in one body, sometimes your own fierce energy.
meaning: Where the lion speaks of authority, the tiger tends to speak of intensity: solitary, striped, hidden in tall grass until it moves. Dreamers describe tigers with awe as often as with fear. A tiger padding beside you may reflect a passion or personal power you are learning to live with; a tiger hunting you can mirror anger, desire or a threat that feels sudden and personal. Notice the distance and whether you could meet its eyes; that is often where the feeling lives.

contexts.reading: A strong part of you, passion or ambition, is becoming an ally rather than a threat.
A sudden danger, real or felt, or anger that might break loose, yours or someone else's.
Energy held back; ask whether the cage protects you or limits you.

lenses.freud: Following Freud's view of wild beasts as passionate impulses, a Freudian reading would ask whose passion the tiger carries and why it had to be disguised.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level the tiger is your own fierce instinct; a Jungian reading asks whether it needs taming, honouring, or simply facing.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; an attack is physical aggression, while a caged tiger watched from safety may involve no interaction at all.
lenses.modern: As a predator, the tiger fits threat simulation (Revonsuo 2000), yet its frequent beauty shows that dreams also process awe and admiration, not only danger.

reflect: Was the tiger more beautiful or more frightening to me?
Where is my own intensity asking for room?
What in my life feels as if it could pounce?

name: Time Travel
summary: Time travel dreams take you into the past or future, often to revisit what was, imagine what might be, or see the present from a new angle.
meaning: Dreams already mix memories from different years, so slipping into another time can feel natural. Travelling back often brings up a period, a place or a version of yourself with something unresolved or treasured: a childhood home, an old friendship, a choice you still think about. Travelling forward can reflect hopes, worries or curiosity about where your path is leading, not a forecast of it. Notice whether you could change anything and how it felt to return. Longing, relief and regret each point somewhere different.

contexts.reading: A return to roots; something from that time may hold comfort or a lesson for now.
Unfinished business or regret; consider what acceptance or repair might look like today.
Hopes and fears about what comes next, pictured as a place you can explore.

lenses.freud: Freud held that dreams draw heavily on childhood, so a trip to the past may be the dream revealing its oldest sources openly.
lenses.jung: Jung saw some dreams as prospective, sketching possible developments rather than predicting events; past and future can meet in the psyche.
lenses.hvdc: Coded through its settings, often familiar or distorted, and its characters, which may include the dreamer at other ages.
lenses.modern: Memory consolidation during sleep draws on recent and remote memories together, which may help explain how dreams blend different periods of life.

reflect: Which time did I visit, and why might it be calling now?
What did I want to change, or to keep?
How did it feel to come back to the present?

name: Tools
summary: Tools stand for capability: the skills, resources and support you have for building, fixing or changing something in your life.
meaning: Tools extend what your hands can do, so dreams of them often concern competence and readiness. A well-stocked toolbox may mirror confidence that you can handle what comes. Reaching for a tool that is missing, broken or wrong for the job is a common frustration image, often echoing a sense that you lack the means, training or support for a task. Being handed tools by someone can reflect mentoring or inheritance. Learning to use an unfamiliar tool may point to a new skill emerging.

contexts.when: You have exactly the right tool
contexts.reading: Often reflects competence, preparation or confidence.

contexts.when: The tool is missing or broken
contexts.reading: May echo lacking resources or support for a task.
Can mirror mentoring, trust or something passed down.

lenses.freud: Freud counted tools and instruments among the objects he read as male symbols; a modern reading might ask more about power and capability.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, tools can stand for the functions of consciousness: the means the ego has for working with life.
lenses.hvdc: Tools are coded in the implements class; completing a task with them can be scored as a success, failing as a failure.
lenses.modern: Problem-solving in dreams often draws on practical waking skills, and tool dreams may show the mind working on a real task.

reflect: What were you trying to build or fix?
Did you have what you needed?
What skill or support would help you right now?

name: Tower
summary: A tower rises above everything around it, often read as aspiration, perspective and isolation: a place to see far or to be set apart.
meaning: Towers lift you out of ordinary life. Climbing one may reflect ambition, the search for an overview or a wish to rise above a situation. At the top, the view can bring clarity or vertigo. Being shut in a tower, as in fairy tales, suggests isolation, or protection that has turned into confinement. A lighthouse offers guidance through darkness. A tower that sways or collapses may mirror fear that a plan or identity built high is less stable than it looks.

contexts.reading: You may be working toward a goal or a wider perspective.
You may feel set apart: protected, but also cut off.
Something you have built may feel less secure than it once did.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading would likely treat the upright tower as a male symbol, linked with potency and ambition.
lenses.jung: Jung built himself a stone tower by a lake as a place of retreat and, in his memoir, tied it to the growth of his inner life; towers suggest the solitary work of individuation.
lenses.hvdc: Towers are architecture objects; standing on top of one is usually coded as an outdoor setting.
lenses.modern: Heights in dreams tend to carry both exhilaration and fear, echoing waking situations of high stakes or exposure.

reflect: Why were you in the tower?
What could you see from the top?
Where in life are you rising, and where are you isolated?

name: Toys
summary: Toys bring back childhood: play, imagination, innocence, and the parts of you that still want to explore without pressure.
meaning: Toys are a doorway to earlier versions of yourself. Finding a beloved toy can mirror longing for simpler times or a wish to reconnect with playfulness. A broken or lost toy may echo something taken from childhood, or a joy you feel you have outgrown. Watching a child play with your toys can bring up questions of inheritance or letting go. Sometimes a toy appears when life has become all duty, as if the psyche were asking for play.

contexts.when: You find a favorite childhood toy
contexts.reading: Often reflects nostalgia, comfort or reconnection with play.

contexts.when: A toy is broken or lost
contexts.reading: May echo grief for something from childhood, or a joy that faded.
Can mirror growing up, letting go or passing something on.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might take the toy back to childhood wishes and to the people who gave, shared or took it away.
lenses.jung: Jung recalled that, in a difficult period, building small stone houses as he had as a boy released his imagination (Memories, Dreams, Reflections, 1962).
lenses.hvdc: Toys are coded in the implements class, which also covers recreational objects.
lenses.modern: Childhood objects can reactivate early memories, and dreams often weave them together with present feelings.

reflect: Which toy was it, and whose?
When did you last play for its own sake?
What part of your younger self wants attention?

name: Train
summary: A train follows fixed tracks toward a destination, often read as a life path already in motion: steady progress, or a course hard to change.
meaning: Trains run on rails, and that is part of their dream meaning: once aboard, the direction is largely set. A pleasant journey may reflect satisfaction with where life is heading, and passing scenery can invite reflection. Being on the wrong train, unable to get off or watching your stop slide past may mirror feeling locked into a course. A runaway train suggests momentum outpacing control. Your fellow passengers, your seat and your ticket can say much about how you feel on the trip.

contexts.reading: You may feel on track and comfortable with your direction.

contexts.when: Wrong train, or cannot get off
contexts.reading: You may feel committed to a path that no longer fits.
Events may be moving faster than you can manage.

lenses.freud: Freud saw journeys as images of life's great departures, and read dreams of missing a train as a form of consolation.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the rails as the collective track of convention, and ask whether you are riding your own line.
lenses.hvdc: Trains are coded in the travel class; fellow passengers are coded as characters.
lenses.modern: Journey dreams may reflect a sense of direction and momentum in waking life; feeling stuck aboard can mirror real constraints.

reflect: Where was the train going?
Could you get off if you wanted to?
Which track is your life on right now?

name: Train Station
summary: A train station is a place of waiting and departure, often read as a junction in life where you choose a direction or wait for the next phase.
meaning: Stations gather timetables, farewells and reunions. In dreams they often appear at junctions: choosing which train to take, waiting for one that never comes, or watching it leave without you. Waiting may mirror a life on hold; a crowded, confusing station, too many options or demands at once. A goodbye on the platform can reflect an ending, while greeting someone may mark a return. A clear departure board suggests clarity about your direction.

contexts.reading: You may be between phases, waiting for something to begin.
You may worry about a missed opportunity, or feel left behind.
An ending or separation may be on your mind.

lenses.freud: Freud read dreams of missing a train as a kind of consolation, and departures as images of life's great leave-takings.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the station as a junction of the psyche, where you choose which track of development to follow.
lenses.hvdc: Stations are architecture objects in an indoor or outdoor setting; the trains are coded in the travel class.
lenses.modern: Missed connections are a familiar theme in stressful dreams and may mirror waking concerns about timing and opportunity.

reflect: Where did you want to go?
Were you on time, early or late?
What are you waiting for right now?

name: Traveling
summary: Traveling is one of the oldest dream images of life as a journey: leaving the familiar, moving through change and arriving somewhere new.
meaning: Journeys in dreams often mirror where you are in life's longer passage. The mode of travel says something: walking is slow and personal, a train follows a set track, a plane leaps ahead, a ship rides the emotional sea. So does the mood. Excitement and curiosity belong to the book's Expansion pattern, an openness to the new; weary, endless travel may echo a period that feels like transit without arrival. Notice your luggage, your companions and whether you knew where you were going.

contexts.reading: Openness to experience; you may be ready for new ideas, people or chapters.
A long transition; ask what arrival would look like and whether you need a rest stop.
Shared direction; notice who travels with you and whether you choose the route together.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might ask what the journey moves away from or toward, the destination standing in for a wish the dreamer does not name.
lenses.jung: The journey is the central image of individuation: the long road toward wholeness, with guides, trials and thresholds along the way.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a location change activity; settings are coded for familiarity, and vehicles such as trains and planes as travel objects.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, travel dreams often borrow recent trips or plans; their emotional tone may reflect how you feel about change.

reflect: Where am I in my own longer journey?
What was I carrying, and with whom was I travelling?
Where would I like to arrive?

name: Treasure
summary: Treasure stands for what is most precious and hard to reach: hidden gifts, true values, and the reward of a search. It is not a forecast of wealth.
meaning: Treasure dreams are about value that is concealed: buried, locked away, guarded or found by chance. The search often matters as much as the find. Digging for treasure can mirror the effort of exploring yourself or a long project; opening a chest may echo discovering a strength, a talent or a love you had not recognized. Treasure that vanishes, or turns out to be worthless, can reflect disappointment or questions about what you truly value. None of this predicts riches; the gold is usually inward.

contexts.reading: Often reflects discovering something valuable in yourself or your life.

contexts.when: You search but cannot find it
contexts.reading: May echo a longing or a quest still unfolding.
Can mirror fears or obstacles standing between you and what you value.

lenses.freud: Freud noted that 'treasure' is a common endearment for a loved person, so a Freudian reading might ask whom the treasure stands for.
lenses.jung: Jung wrote of the 'treasure hard to attain', guarded by a dragon in myth, as an image of the Self won through the hero's struggle (Symbols of Transformation).
lenses.hvdc: Treasure is coded with money-related objects; finding it unexpectedly can be coded as good fortune.
lenses.modern: Quest and discovery dreams often accompany periods of learning or change, when the mind is seeking what matters most.

reflect: What was the treasure, exactly?
What stood in the way of reaching it?
What do you value most that you may have overlooked?

name: Trickster
summary: The trickster brings chaos, mischief and surprise, upsetting plans to reveal what is rigid, false or ready to change.
meaning: Tricksters show up as jokers, con artists, clowns or animals with human cunning. They break rules, play pranks and turn situations upside down, which can feel infuriating in the dream. Yet the disruption often exposes something: a plan that was too rigid, a pride that needed puncturing, a truth no one wanted to say. If a trickster fools you, ask where you might be fooling yourself. If you are the trickster, the dream may be inviting more humour, flexibility or creative rule-breaking into a life that has grown too serious.

contexts.reading: Ask where you may be ignoring signs, or where trust is being tested in waking life.
Often a release of tension; humour may help with something you are taking very seriously.
This may reflect a wish to break free of rules, or a need for play and spontaneity.

lenses.freud: Freud wrote that jokes, like dreams, let forbidden thoughts slip past the inner censor; a trickster may carry that same release.
lenses.jung: Jung wrote on the trickster as an archetype of disorder and renewal, a reminder of what is undeveloped and of the creative power in chaos.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a human character, or as an animal if the trickster takes animal form; tricks and deceptions may be coded as non-physical aggression.
lenses.modern: Illogical turns are common in dreams; the looser associations of REM sleep may be part of why tricksters feel at home there.

reflect: What did the trickster disrupt?
Where are you taking yourself too seriously?
What truth might the joke be telling?

name: Truck
summary: A truck carries heavy loads, often read as burdens, responsibilities and the hard work of moving something important forward.
meaning: Trucks are built for weight. In dreams they often carry what you are hauling through life: duties, commitments, other people's needs or a large project. Driving a heavy truck steadily can reflect capability under load; losing control of one may mirror fear that responsibilities have grown too big to steer. A truck bearing down on you suggests pressure arriving fast. A moving truck often accompanies change: packing up a phase of life to carry it somewhere new.

contexts.reading: You may be carrying significant responsibility, perhaps carrying it well.

contexts.when: A truck bearing down on you
contexts.reading: Pressure or demands may feel as if they are closing in.
You may be preparing for a change of home, role or chapter.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might look at strength and force, and at the load the dreamer wishes to deliver or to unload.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might ask what the cargo holds: burdens taken on from others, or contents of your own psyche carried unopened.
lenses.hvdc: Trucks are coded in the travel class; a collision is coded as a misfortune.
lenses.modern: Heavy vehicles may embody waking stress about workload, consistent with the continuity hypothesis.

reflect: What was the truck carrying?
Who was driving, and could they handle the load?
Which burden could you set down or share?

name: Tunnel
summary: A tunnel is a passage through darkness, often read as a hard stretch you must go through, with the hope of light at the end.
meaning: Tunnels are passages, not places to stay: they carry you under a mountain, beneath water or through the earth. In dreams they often mark a phase that feels narrow, dark or hard to see through, a transition with no view of the destination. Light ahead brings relief; a tunnel that narrows, floods or closes behind you may reflect pressure or a fear of being stuck. Moving through steadily can show endurance, while crawling suggests effort against close limits.

contexts.reading: A hard stretch may be nearing its end, or hope may be returning.
You may feel squeezed by circumstances or short of options.
You may be carried through a difficult period with some momentum.

lenses.freud: Freud linked passing through narrow spaces in dreams with fantasies about the womb and birth; a tunnel invites that reading.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the tunnel as a night sea journey, the hero's passage through darkness before renewal.
lenses.hvdc: A built passage; when it is unclear whether the scene counts as indoor or outdoor, it is coded as ambiguous.
lenses.modern: Enclosed passages lend themselves to threat simulation; a tunnel may give shape to a waking stretch that feels long and uncertain.

reflect: Could you see the end of the tunnel?
Which hard stretch in your life feels like this passage?
What helps you keep moving when you cannot see far ahead?

name: Turtle
summary: The turtle or tortoise is widely linked with patience, long life, protection and slow, steady progress, and in many myths with the earth itself.
meaning: A turtle carries its home on its back and moves at its own pace, so dreams often use it for patience, protection and steady progress; some creation stories even rest the world on a turtle's shell. A turtle withdrawing into its shell may reflect a need to retreat and stay safe for a while, or a habit of hiding when life gets loud. Baby sea turtles racing to the water often feel hopeful, a journey begun against the odds.

contexts.reading: Patience; progress may be slower than you want, but it is real.
A need for protection, or a pattern of withdrawing when things feel unsafe.

contexts.when: Baby turtles head for the sea
contexts.reading: A fragile new beginning that needs courage and a little luck.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the shell as a wish for a safe enclosure, a return to protection after feeling exposed.
lenses.jung: In Jungian terms the turtle can embody the slow wisdom of nature and the Self; world-turtle myths amplify its sense of grounding.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; often no interaction is coded, and the dream is described by its setting and the dreamer's emotions.
lenses.modern: Turtle dreams often surface when patience or self-protection is a waking theme, as the continuity hypothesis would predict.

reflect: Where do I need to slow down and trust steady progress?
When do I retreat into my shell, and does it help?
What fragile beginning needs my courage?

name: Umbrella
summary: An umbrella stands for protection: shielding yourself from emotional weather, and how prepared you feel for what is coming.
meaning: Since rain so often carries emotion in dreams, an umbrella can show how you handle feeling: keeping dry, staying composed, or holding difficult moods at a distance. Sharing one may mirror closeness and care. An umbrella that turns inside out, breaks or is forgotten often echoes feeling unprepared for stress, or a sense that your usual defenses are no longer enough. Sometimes putting the umbrella down and letting the rain fall can feel like relief.

contexts.reading: Often reflects closeness, protection or support in a relationship.
May echo defenses that feel overwhelmed, or stress outpacing your preparation.

contexts.when: You choose to walk in the rain
contexts.reading: Can mirror a readiness to feel what you have been holding back.

lenses.freud: Freud included umbrellas among elongated objects he read as male symbols, pointing to their opening; today this is one reading among many.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the umbrella may be the ego's shelter from the unconscious, useful until it keeps you from what you need to feel.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an object; the rain or storm around it falls under the nature class.
lenses.modern: Protective images often appear when people anticipate stress, as dreams rehearse coping with what may come.

reflect: What were you sheltering from?
Who was under the umbrella with you?
What feeling might you let yourself experience?

name: Unable to Run
summary: A common frustration dream: you try to run but your legs are heavy, slow or will not move. It often mirrors feeling held back just when you need to act.
meaning: Few dream experiences are as maddening as wading through invisible syrup while danger approaches. The dream often appears alongside Pursuit, but the image stands on its own: urgency meeting a body that will not cooperate. It may echo a waking situation where effort is not turning into motion, whether exhaustion, a decision you keep postponing or an obstacle you cannot name. Some dreamers find that when they stop forcing, they can walk, fly or simply wake; that release can be the message.

contexts.reading: Pressure plus powerlessness: where do you feel pushed yet stuck, perhaps by a deadline or someone's expectations?
Can point to fatigue or a burden you are carrying; the body may be asking for rest more than speed.

contexts.when: You stop struggling and it eases
contexts.reading: A shift from force to acceptance that often brings unexpected freedom, in the dream and outside it.

lenses.freud: Freud wrote about the dream sensation of inhibited movement and read it as a conflict of will: one impulse pushing forward while another says no.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the stalled legs may belong to a part of you that disagrees with the direction the ego is rushing in.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a failure when the dreamer strives and cannot, or a misfortune when an outside obstacle intervenes.
lenses.modern: One popular idea links the sensation to the muscle atonia of REM sleep reaching awareness, though this is difficult to test directly.

reflect: Where do I feel I am trying hard but not moving?
What is part of me reluctant to move toward?
What did I need in that moment, instead of speed?

name: Unable to Scream
summary: Trying to scream and making no sound is a widely shared dream of powerlessness, often mirroring a feeling that your voice is not being heard.
meaning: Danger approaches, you open your mouth to shout, and nothing comes out, or only a whisper. Few dream moments feel so helpless. Emotionally, the scene often mirrors situations where speaking up feels impossible or pointless: a boss who does not listen, a family role that leaves no room, a fear you have not voiced. It often appears alongside Pursuit. Notice what you were trying to say and to whom. Some dreamers find their voice later in the same dream or in later ones, a change worth noting.

contexts.reading: Fear of being unsupported; who would you like to hear you, and do they know?
Concern for another person that you have not expressed; perhaps it is time.
A shift toward self-expression, often a sign of growing confidence.

lenses.freud: Freud related inhibited movement in dreams to a conflict of will; a silenced scream may show one wish to cry out meeting another that forbids it.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the voiceless self may be a part of you not yet allowed to speak, seeking a place in conscious life.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a failure when the dreamer strives to call out and cannot; apprehension is usually coded as the emotion.
lenses.modern: One idea links the experience to the muscle atonia of REM sleep; if you wake unable to move or speak for a moment, that is sleep paralysis, common and brief.

reflect: Where do I feel unheard right now?
What was I trying to say, and to whom?
What would help me speak up?

name: Underworld
summary: The underworld, the realm below in many myths, is often read as a descent into hidden depths: grief, memory, the unconscious and the transformation that can follow.
meaning: Many myths tell of journeys below: heroes who descend in search of wisdom, lovers who follow the lost, seeds that wait underground until spring. Dreams of an underworld often share this shape. A descent may coincide with grief, low mood or deep reflection, when ordinary life feels far above. What matters is often what you seek there, whom you meet and what you bring back. Returning to daylight, even changed, is a common and hopeful turn in such dreams.

contexts.reading: You may be ready to explore a difficult memory or feeling.
Grief, ancestry or unfinished words may be present for you.
You may be emerging from a hard period with something learned.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the world below as the realm of the repressed, where the dead and the forbidden are kept.
lenses.jung: Jung's earliest remembered dream, told in his memoir, led down stone steps beneath a meadow into a hidden chamber; such descents are central to Jungian work with the unconscious.
lenses.hvdc: The system codes only what is described, typically an unfamiliar setting; people who have died are coded as dead characters.
lenses.modern: Descent imagery may accompany grief or low mood, consistent with emotional processing in REM sleep; it does not predict anything.

reflect: What were you seeking below?
Whom did you meet there?
What did you bring back, or hope to?

name: Unicorn
summary: The unicorn is widely read as purity, rarity and wonder, the magical and hard to find, and as hope or idealism.
meaning: In medieval legend the unicorn could be approached only through gentleness and innocence, and its horn was said to cleanse poison; today it often stands for wonder, magic and the hard to find. Dream unicorns may arrive when you are longing for something pure, rare or ideal: a perfect relationship, a dream job, a version of yourself. Meeting one can bring joy and hope. A unicorn that runs away may mirror an ideal that feels unreachable, or a question about whether it is realistic.

contexts.reading: Hope, wonder, or contact with something rare and precious in yourself.
An ideal that feels out of reach; perhaps worth looking at more gently.
Trust in your imagination and idealism, or a wish to escape the ordinary.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the single horn as symbolised desire, and the unicorn's gentleness with the innocent as a wish to keep longing pure.
lenses.jung: Jung traced the unicorn through alchemy and religious art in Psychology and Alchemy (1944), as an image of spirit and of opposites united.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an imaginary creature in the Dead and Imaginary class; riding it is an activity, and a gentle approach is friendliness.
lenses.modern: Unicorn dreams often draw on childhood imagery and popular culture, and usually carry wonder, longing or other positive emotion.

reflect: What ideal am I longing for?
Is it truly out of reach, or simply rare?
Where could I let in more wonder?

name: Uniform
summary: A uniform stands for belonging and role: duty, discipline, authority, and the parts of you that blend in with a group.
meaning: A uniform tells everyone what you are there to do. In dreams it can mirror pride in a role, or the sense that the role has swallowed the person. Wearing an old school uniform often returns the dreamer to a time of rules and evaluation, especially under current pressure. A uniform that no longer fits may echo a role you are outgrowing; facing someone in uniform can reflect your relationship with authority, rules or being checked on.

contexts.when: You wear a school uniform again
contexts.reading: Often linked to feeling tested or judged, as in school days.

contexts.when: You wear a uniform with pride
contexts.reading: May reflect belonging, purpose or commitment to a team.
Can echo concern about rules, permission or being evaluated.

lenses.freud: Freud observed that dreams can represent nakedness through clothes and uniforms; a uniform may cover an exposure the dreamer would rather not show.
lenses.jung: A uniform is the persona at its most collective: on the subjective level it asks where your role ends and you begin.
lenses.hvdc: Coded in the clothing class; a uniform also helps coders identify characters by occupation.
lenses.modern: Work and school uniforms carry waking routines into sleep, often alongside evaluation stress.

reflect: Which role did the uniform belong to?
Did it feel like an honor or a disguise?
Where do you feel you have to fit a mold?

name: Unknown Child
summary: An unknown child often points to something new, vulnerable or unfinished in you: potential, playfulness, or a need for care.
meaning: A child you have never met is one of the dream's most open images. It may be a new project, a fresh start, a part of you that is still innocent, or an old hurt that never got the attention it needed. How you treat the child matters as much as the child itself. Caring for it suggests readiness to nurture something; ignoring or losing it may show that something tender is being neglected. A strangely calm or wise child can feel like a guide, offering a simple truth adults overcomplicate.

contexts.when: You care for or protect the child
contexts.reading: You may be ready to take on something new, or to treat yourself more kindly.

contexts.when: The child is lost, crying or alone
contexts.reading: Often a sensitive need going unmet; ask what you have been too busy to tend.

contexts.when: The child speaks wisely or leads you
contexts.reading: This may reflect intuition, or a simpler view that cuts through current complications.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might link an unknown child to wishes about the future, or to the dreamer's own childhood returning in disguise.
lenses.jung: Jung wrote of the child archetype as futurity and new possibility; a strange, wise child may point toward the Self.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a stranger character with the system's age code for child or baby, so the balance of adults and children in your dreams can be seen.
lenses.modern: New responsibilities, creative projects and caregiving often bring child figures into dreams, consistent with the continuity of waking concerns.

reflect: How did you feel toward the child?
What in your life is new, small and still forming?
What would the child need from you next?

name: Vampire
summary: The vampire is often read as something that drains your energy, and also as seduction, hunger, or a fear of being consumed.
meaning: The vampire of novels and films is charming, ageless and hungry, so in dreams it often blends attraction and threat. It may mirror a relationship, job or habit that drains you while seeming irresistible. It can also reflect your own hunger for attention, youth or connection, and the guilt that comes with it. Because vampires shun daylight, the image can point to something that thrives only in secrecy. Becoming a vampire may reflect a fear of turning into what drains you.

contexts.reading: Something alluring that may also be draining you.
Fear of becoming what drains you, or guilt about your own needs.
Bringing a hidden situation into the open takes away much of its power.

lenses.freud: Freud's follower Ernest Jones, in On the Nightmare (1931), read vampire legends as disguised expressions of forbidden longing and of mixed feelings toward the dead.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading sees the vampire as a shadow figure: hungers we disown, returning as something that feeds on others.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an imaginary creature in the Dead and Imaginary class; a bite or attack is coded as physical aggression.
lenses.modern: Vampire dreams often draw on fiction, and may follow periods of exhaustion or a draining relationship, as continuity would expect.

reflect: What in my life drains me while drawing me in?
What hunger in me do I find hard to admit?
What might lose its power if brought into the light?

name: Village
summary: A village suggests close community, simplicity and roots: a smaller world where everyone knows everyone.
meaning: Villages are human in scale: a square, a few streets, familiar faces. Dreaming of one may reflect a longing for belonging, slower rhythms or a return to roots. A welcoming village can feel like coming home. The same closeness can also feel watchful, and a village where everyone stares may mirror feeling judged by a small circle. An abandoned village carries the quiet of what has been left behind. Notice whether you are a resident, a visitor or only passing through.

contexts.reading: You may be longing for closeness, simplicity or community.
You may feel scrutinised by the people closest to you.
Something from your past or your roots may feel distant now.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might link the village to the small world of childhood and the family figures who filled it.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the village as a contained community of inner figures, or as an ancestral layer of the psyche.
lenses.hvdc: Villages are coded in the regions class, usually as outdoor settings, familiar or unfamiliar by whether you know them.
lenses.modern: Smaller-scale settings may reflect a wish to simplify, consistent with dreams working over present social needs.

reflect: Did you belong in this village, or were you visiting?
How did the people there treat you?
What would a simpler, closer life look like for you?

name: Void
summary: A void is space without features, often read as emptiness, uncertainty or a pause before something new takes shape.
meaning: Some dreams have no setting at all: only blackness, whiteness or an endless empty space. A void can feel terrifying, peaceful or strangely neutral. It may mirror numbness, exhaustion or a time when old structures have fallen away and new ones have not yet formed. It can also be a clearing: quiet after noise, a blank page. Notice whether you were floating, falling or standing still, and whether anything appeared in the emptiness, such as a light, a sound or a voice.

contexts.reading: You may feel unanchored, or afraid of losing direction.
You may need rest from stimulation, or be ready for a fresh start.
A new idea, feeling or direction may be taking shape.

lenses.freud: Freud's followers explored blank dreams; Lewin (1946) proposed a 'dream screen' echoing the infant falling asleep at the breast, a reading of the void as longed-for rest.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the void as the unformed ground of the psyche, an emptiness that comes before new creation, or as compensation for an overfull life.
lenses.hvdc: A featureless space is coded as an ambiguous setting, or as no setting when no place is described at all.
lenses.modern: Featureless dreams are sometimes reported near sleep onset; their feeling tone may reflect fatigue, calm or a mind with little to process.

reflect: How did the emptiness feel?
Were you floating, falling or still?
What space in your life is waiting to be filled, or to be left empty a little longer?

name: Vomiting
summary: Vomiting in a dream often reflects a need to get rid of something: an experience, a feeling or a situation you cannot stomach.
meaning: Unpleasant as it is, vomiting in a dream often carries relief. It can point to something you need to expel: resentment, guilt, a toxic situation or words you have held in. Feeling nauseous without vomiting may reflect something you are struggling to accept. Vomiting in public can echo embarrassment or a fear of losing control in front of others. Helping someone who is sick may show care for them, or concern that they are struggling with something. The image concerns emotion and release, not your digestion or your health.

contexts.reading: Often a release; what have you been holding in that needs to come out?
This may reflect a situation or decision you find hard to accept.
This can echo a fear of embarrassment or of losing control.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might link vomiting to disgust, which Freud saw as one of the forces that push unwanted wishes away.
lenses.jung: Jung might see expulsion as part of purification: the psyche ridding itself of what it cannot digest.
lenses.hvdc: Vomiting is coded as a bodily misfortune, with the setting and any onlookers recorded separately.
lenses.modern: Nausea in dreams can echo real stomach discomfort during sleep, and the emotion of disgust often tracks waking situations that feel wrong.

reflect: What did you need to get rid of in the dream?
What in your life can you not stomach?
What would release look like for you?

name: Vulture
summary: The vulture is commonly read as waiting, endings and something feeding on what is left, and also as cleansing, patience and recycling.
meaning: Vultures circle patiently and feed on what has died, so dreams use them for endings, and for feeling watched by someone waiting for you to fail. Circling vultures can mirror dread, or exploitation: people who profit from others' losses. Yet vultures do essential work, clearing away what is dead before it spreads disease, and in ancient Egypt a vulture goddess was a protective mother. The image can point to something finished that needs to be cleared.

contexts.reading: A feeling of being watched or waited on, or dread about something ending.
Something finished being cleared away, or someone profiting from a loss.
Patience, or a hard truth about what is already over.

lenses.freud: Freud's study of Leonardo (1910) built on a childhood memory he took to involve a vulture (the bird was in fact a kite) and linked it with the mother.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading sees the vulture as death and renewal, the devouring that prepares new life; Egypt's vulture mother amplifies this.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character, several as a group; circling without contact involves no coded interaction.
lenses.modern: Vulture dreams often appear around endings at work or in relationships, as the brain processes loss and the fear of being exploited.

reflect: What in my life is already over and needs clearing?
Do I feel someone is waiting for me to fail?
Am I feeding on someone else's loss, or being fed upon?

name: Wall
summary: A wall marks a boundary, protective or confining, and in dreams it often shows where you feel blocked or what you are keeping out.
meaning: Walls divide, protect and contain. The same wall can feel like shelter or a prison depending on which side you are on and what you want. A high wall in your path may mirror an obstacle or a limit set by someone else; walls closing in, pressure building. A crack or collapse can be frightening, yet it may also show defences softening. Building a wall suggests a need for protection or distance; climbing one, determination to get past a barrier.

contexts.reading: An obstacle may call for another route, some help or patience.
Pressure or obligations may feel as if they leave you no room.
Defences or limits may be changing, which can feel both risky and freeing.

lenses.freud: Freud repeated a traditional view that houses with smooth walls stand for men and those with ledges and balconies for women; a Freudian reading attends to such details.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see walls as the ego's defences, with shadow material waiting behind them to be recognised.
lenses.hvdc: An architecture object; a wall that halts your efforts may also figure in a coded failure.
lenses.modern: Barriers are common in stress dreams and may reflect waking frustrations, consistent with the continuity hypothesis.

reflect: Which side of the wall were you on?
What was the wall keeping in, or keeping out?
Where in your life would a door in this wall help?

name: Wallet
summary: A wallet holds both money and identity, so it often stands for your sense of security, self-worth and who you are in the world.
meaning: Unlike loose cash, a wallet carries cards, papers and small personal things: proof of who you are. That is why losing one in a dream can feel so disorienting. It may echo a period when your role, independence or self-image feels exposed or in question. Finding a lost wallet, or having it returned, can mirror restored confidence or trust. An empty wallet often speaks of depletion more than money: feeling you have little left to give.

contexts.reading: Often linked to feeling exposed, unprepared or unsure of your footing in a role.
Can echo a sense that something of yours (credit, energy, identity) is being taken.
May mirror trust restored, or a part of yourself coming back after a hard time.

lenses.freud: Freud counted pockets and cases among the hollow receptacles in his symbolism; a reader today might ask what felt most precious inside.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, a wallet can hold the persona's credentials: the identity you show the world, and its fragility.
lenses.hvdc: A wallet is usually coded with money-related objects; losing it can be scored as a misfortune.
lenses.modern: Losing essentials is a familiar dream theme; continuity research would look for waking moments of feeling exposed or underprepared.

reflect: What was inside the wallet that mattered most?
Where do you feel exposed, or unsure of your footing?
What would help you feel secure in who you are?

name: War
summary: War dreams are distressing and common, especially in tense times. They usually reflect conflict, stress or worry about the world, not a prediction.
meaning: Sirens, soldiers, a city under threat: war dreams carry conflict on the largest scale. For most people they mirror tension closer to home, a battle at work, a family divided, a struggle within yourself between competing needs, or the weight of news from real conflicts. Notice your role. Fighting, hiding, helping the wounded or fleeing each suggest a different way of meeting conflict. For people who have lived through war, dreams may replay real events; if they keep returning and disturb your sleep, a professional can help.

contexts.reading: A sense of duty, or of being drafted into a struggle not of your choosing; whose fight are you in?
A wish for safety and distance from conflict; ask where you need refuge right now.
A movement toward resolution; you may be ready to step out of a long conflict.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the warring sides as conflicting wishes, the battle staging an inner struggle too charged to face directly.
lenses.jung: War can picture the clash between the ego and the shadow, or between opposites seeking reconciliation in the psyche.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as aggression, often physical and involving groups of characters; in men's norms, aggression is more frequent than friendliness.
lenses.modern: Threat simulation theory (Revonsuo 2000) sees such scenes as rehearsal; Levin and Nielsen (2007) note that distress and real trauma can make nightmares more frequent.

reflect: What conflict am I caught up in right now?
What was my role in the war?
What would peace look like for me?

name: Wedding
summary: A wedding often symbolises commitment, union and transition: joining two things, two people or two parts of yourself.
meaning: Weddings in dreams are not always about marriage. They often mark a commitment or a union: to a person, a project, a new role or a decision. Joy and celebration can reflect readiness for that step, while panic, a missing partner, the wrong bride or groom, or a ceremony that falls apart may reflect doubts, fear of losing freedom or pressure from others' expectations. Attending someone else's wedding can reflect changes in your relationship with them. Because weddings are public, these dreams may also touch on how others see your choices.

contexts.reading: Often a sense of readiness and harmony with a commitment you are making.

contexts.when: Something goes wrong or you want to run
contexts.reading: This may voice doubts or pressure; whose expectations are shaping this choice?
Consider the qualities they represent; you may be uniting with them in yourself.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see wishes for union alongside anxieties about lost freedom or about the parents' approval.
lenses.jung: Jung saw the sacred marriage of alchemy as a union of opposites; a dream wedding can picture inner integration, such as joining with the anima or animus.
lenses.hvdc: Coded through what is present: characters, often groups of mixed sex, friendly interactions, clothing such as the dress, and the setting.
lenses.modern: Engagements, family weddings and decisions about commitment often bring weddings into dreams, consistent with the continuity of waking concerns.

reflect: What, or whom, were you committing to?
How did you feel at the ceremony?
What would make this commitment feel right?

name: Wedding dress
summary: A wedding dress speaks of commitment, transformation and expectation: stepping into a new identity, and the hopes or pressures around it.
meaning: This image can visit anyone, engaged or not, because it is less about marriage itself than about a threshold. Wearing the dress can mirror readiness for a deep commitment, to a person, a project or a new self. A dress that does not fit, is stained or cannot be found often echoes doubts or the weight of other people's expectations. Seeing someone else in it may stir longing, comparison or memory, especially of a relationship that took a different path.

contexts.reading: May reflect readiness for a commitment or a new chapter.

contexts.when: It does not fit or is damaged
contexts.reading: Often mirrors doubts, pressure or fear that something will go wrong.
Can stir longing, comparison, or feelings about a relationship that changed.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might look for the wish and the fear bound up together in the image of the bride.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, the bridal dress can mark the inner marriage, the union of opposites Jung saw as central to individuation.
lenses.hvdc: Coded in the clothing class; a wedding setting and its characters are coded separately.
lenses.modern: Weddings in waking life, your own or others', often feed these dreams, along with feelings about commitment and family expectations.

reflect: What did wearing it feel like?
What commitment, of any kind, is on your mind?
Whose expectations did the dress carry?

name: Werewolf
summary: The werewolf is often read as a split between the civilised self and wild instinct: a part of you, or of someone else, that changes without warning.
meaning: A werewolf is a person by day and a beast under the full moon, so it suits fears and feelings about change that runs out of control. It may mirror someone whose moods shift suddenly, kind one moment and frightening the next, or your own anger, appetite or desire that seems to take over. Turning into a werewolf yourself can reflect a fear of losing control, or a longing to let your wild side out. Who you were with when the change came matters.

contexts.when: Someone you know turns into one
contexts.reading: Unpredictable moods, or a hidden side of someone close.
Fear of losing control, or instinct demanding expression.

contexts.when: You hide from it under the full moon
contexts.reading: Dread of a recurring situation you know is coming.

lenses.freud: Ernest Jones, in On the Nightmare (1931), treated werewolf legends as disguised forms of forbidden impulses and guilt; a Freudian reading looks for what the change hides.
lenses.jung: In Jungian terms the werewolf is the shadow breaking through the persona: instinct denied until it erupts.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an imaginary creature in the Dead and Imaginary class; an attack is coded as physical aggression toward the dreamer.
lenses.modern: Werewolf dreams often follow horror films or tense times with someone unpredictable; threat simulation and emotion processing both play a part.

reflect: Whose moods change without warning in my life?
When do I feel I am losing control?
What part of my wild nature wants room?

name: Whale
summary: The whale is often read as depth, vastness and deep wisdom, and in old stories as being swallowed into the depths and returned.
meaning: Whales are the largest beings most of us can imagine, moving slowly through dark water and singing to each other across great distances. Dreams use them for depth: deep feeling, deep memory, a presence far bigger than the self. A whale surfacing often brings awe, like contact with something ancient. Being swallowed, as in the story of Jonah, can reflect a time of being overwhelmed that is also a passage, an inward journey you come back from changed.

contexts.reading: Contact with deep feeling, or a sense of awe and perspective.
Feeling engulfed by a situation or mood, perhaps a time of inner retreat and return.
A deep, wordless longing or connection that is hard to put into language.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see in being swallowed a wish to return to the enclosure of the womb, or a fear of being engulfed by a parent.
lenses.jung: Jung read the hero swallowed by a sea monster, as in Jonah, as the night sea journey: a descent into the unconscious before renewal.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character in an outdoor setting; being swallowed counts as aggression if the whale seems to act against you, otherwise as a misfortune.
lenses.modern: Awe-filled dreams show that dreaming processes expansive, positive emotion as well as fear; continuity points to a waking sense of something larger than you.

reflect: What feels vast and deep in my life right now?
Where do I feel swallowed, and what might I learn inside?
What wordless longing am I carrying?

name: Window
summary: A window is a view: how you see the world and how the world sees you, a boundary that lets light in without letting you through.
meaning: Windows connect inside and outside while keeping them apart. Looking out may reflect perspective, longing or the wish to join a life you watch from a distance. Someone looking in can mirror feeling observed or exposed. Clean glass suggests clarity; dirty, fogged or barred windows, a limited or clouded view of a situation. A broken window can feel alarming, yet it may also mean that a barrier between you and something outside has finally given way.

contexts.when: Gazing out at a wide view
contexts.reading: You may be gaining perspective, or longing for a broader life.
You may feel watched, judged or less private than you would like.
A boundary may feel breached, or a protective distance may be ending.

lenses.freud: If the house can stand for the body, as Freud accepted, a Freudian reading might treat windows as its openings and ask what wishes to enter or escape.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading sees the window as the meeting point of inner and outer worlds, the ego looking out or being glimpsed from outside.
lenses.hvdc: An architecture object; whether you stand inside looking out or outside looking in decides if the setting is coded indoor or outdoor.
lenses.modern: Watching events through glass may reflect waking situations you observe without feeling part of, in line with the continuity hypothesis.

reflect: Were you inside looking out, or outside looking in?
What did the view show you?
Where in life are you watching rather than taking part?

name: Winning
summary: Winning is a widely shared dream of success and recognition: crossing the line first, taking the prize, being chosen.
meaning: Victory dreams can be pure pleasure, a taste of what success feels like, and that alone can be encouraging. They belong to Ascent: rising, achieving, being lifted by others' applause. The context matters. Winning something you have worked for may reflect growing confidence; winning by luck, a wish for relief or rescue; winning against someone you know, a rivalry or a need to be acknowledged by them. Notice how the win felt. Hollow victories, where the prize disappoints or nobody notices, are telling in their own way.

contexts.reading: Confidence and readiness; the dream may be rehearsing a success you are working toward.
Achievement that does not satisfy; ask what you actually want beyond the prize.
A wish for ease, freedom or rescue from pressure; consider what you would change if you could.

lenses.freud: Winning is close to pure wish fulfilment in Freud's sense: the dream grants the success or recognition the dreamer longs for.
lenses.jung: Victory can belong to the hero's journey; Jungians would also watch for inflation, when the ego identifies too closely with the triumph.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a success when the dreamer reaches a goal through effort; a pure windfall is coded as a good fortune instead.
lenses.modern: By the continuity hypothesis, winning dreams often accompany competitions, interviews or goals; positive dream emotion can colour the morning's mood.

reflect: What success am I hoping for right now?
How did the win truly feel?
Who did I want to see me win?

name: Wise Old Person
summary: A wise old person often appears as a guide at a moment of need, carrying insight, perspective and your own deeper knowing.
meaning: The elder with good advice is one of the oldest figures in stories and dreams. They may appear as a hermit, a grandparent, a teacher or a stranger with kind eyes, often when you face a crossroads or feel lost. Their words can be simple, puzzling or absent. The dream may be giving voice to wisdom you already have but have not yet trusted. Notice whether you listen or argue, and whether the advice feels warm or stern. A wise figure who turns harsh or confusing may reflect a struggle between old certainties and new understanding.

contexts.reading: Often your own inner judgement speaking; write the words down, they may prove useful.

contexts.when: They speak in riddles or stay silent
contexts.reading: The answer may need time, or you may need to stop seeking it outside yourself.
This can reflect growing confidence in your experience, or a role guiding others.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see an idealised parent, the all-knowing figure of early childhood, returning when the dreamer wants rescue.
lenses.jung: Jung described the wise old man as an archetype of spirit and meaning that appears when insight is needed; the wise old woman often accompanies the great mother.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an adult character by sex and identity, often a stranger; helpful advice is coded as friendliness toward the dreamer.
lenses.modern: Dreams can recombine memories into a guiding figure, and research on sleep and insight suggests sleep sometimes helps people see a problem afresh.

reflect: What did the elder tell or show you?
Do you already know the answer you are seeking?
Who in your life offers this kind of wisdom?

name: Witch
summary: A witch often embodies hidden power, transformation and the feared or rejected sides of feminine strength, in a frightening or a helpful form.
meaning: Witches in dreams can be terrifying or fascinating. As frightening figures they may give shape to a controlling or harsh influence, to envy, or to a fear of power used against you. As helpful figures, healers or herb gatherers, they can point to intuition, independence and a capacity for change that does not follow the usual rules. Folk tales gave the witch both faces, and dreams often do the same. Ask whether the witch wanted to harm you, test you or teach you, and whether some part of her power belongs to you.

contexts.reading: Often fear of a controlling influence, or of your own anger turned into a monster.
This can reflect trust in intuition and in unconventional ways of solving a problem.
This may point to claiming power, independence or creativity you have held back.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the witch as the frightening side of the mother, split off from the loving one the child wants to keep.
lenses.jung: Jung saw the witch as an image of the negative mother, devouring or bewitching; in other tales she is the wise woman who knows what others do not.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as a human character by sex and age, usually a female stranger; her magic is coded through what she does, such as threats or help.
lenses.modern: Fairy tale figures enter dreams from memory and media; the feelings they carry, threat or wonder, link them to current concerns.

reflect: Did the witch frighten, test or help you?
What power in your life feels dangerous to use?
What would you brew if you could?

name: Wolf
summary: The wolf is widely seen as instinct, loyalty to the pack and wild freedom, and in folk tales as the predator at the edge of the forest.
meaning: The wolf has two faces in human imagination: the loyal pack animal and the hungry stranger of fairy tales. Dreams draw on both. A wolf watching from the trees can feel like a warning, or like a wild part of you asking for attention. A pack may reflect belonging, family or teamwork, and also group pressure. Howling at night often comes with loneliness or longing. If you run with the wolves rather than from them, the dream may be about freedom and trusting your instincts.

contexts.reading: Something wild or unknown is noticing you, or you are noticing your own need for solitude.
Group pressure, gossip, or many demands closing in at once.
Belonging, shared purpose and trust in your own instincts.

lenses.freud: Freud's 'Wolf Man' case (1918) centred on a child's dream of white wolves sitting in a tree, which Freud connected with the patient's father and early fears.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading may see the wolf as shadow, the hungry, untamed side the persona hides, or as a guide when the dreamer runs alongside it.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character, a pack as a group; a chase is coded as aggression one step below a physical attack.
lenses.modern: In threat simulation terms (Revonsuo 2000) a pursuing pack rehearses escape; the continuity view would look for a social pressure behind it.

reflect: Was I hunted by the wolf, watched by it, or running with it?
Where do I feel like a lone wolf, and is that by choice?
What wild part of me wants more room?

name: Working
summary: Work dreams are among the most common everyday dreams: tasks, colleagues and deadlines carried into sleep, often with a twist.
meaning: Many work dreams are simply the day continuing: the inbox, the meeting, the problem you did not solve before leaving. Yet the twist is often the message. An office that turns into a maze, a colleague who becomes a childhood friend, a task that cannot be finished: these details show how the work feels, not just what it is. Notice whether you felt competent, overwhelmed, bored or proud. Returning to an old job can point to a lesson or feeling from that time that has become relevant again.

contexts.reading: Overload; the dream may be asking for boundaries between work and rest.
An earlier version of you, or an old dynamic, may be active again in a current situation.
Satisfaction and purpose, or a glimpse of the kind of work you want more of.

lenses.freud: Freud called the day's leftover impressions day residue; a Freudian reading asks which wish has borrowed today's tasks as its costume.
lenses.jung: On the subjective level, colleagues may be aspects of you; Jungians would ask whether the persona of your role is crowding out the rest of you.
lenses.hvdc: Coded by activity (verbal, physical, thinking) and by characters, often occupational or known; the workplace is a familiar indoor setting.
lenses.modern: Work themes illustrate the continuity hypothesis well: the people and concerns that fill your days tend to fill your dreams too.

reflect: How does my work feel to me right now?
What detail in the dream was strange, and what might it mean?
Where do I need a clearer line between work and rest?

name: Worm
summary: Worms are often read as humble renewal, the work that turns decay into fertile soil, and sometimes as feeling small, or something eating away inside.
meaning: Earthworms do quiet, essential work underground, turning what has died into soil where new things grow, so a worm dream can carry slow renewal and the value of humble effort. But worms also burrow into fruit, and many people find them unsettling; then the image may point to doubt, guilt or a worry eating away from inside. Feeling 'like a worm' is also an old image of low self-worth. Your feeling, curiosity or revulsion, shows which side is speaking.

contexts.reading: Quiet renewal; something is being composted into new growth.
Doubt or worry spoiling something that looks fine on the outside.
Low self-worth, or being treated as small; it may be worth questioning.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might link burrowing worms to bodily sensations, or to hidden guilt working its way toward the surface.
lenses.jung: In Jungian amplification the worm is kin to the dragon (Old English wyrm meant both): instinct at its humblest, where transformation can begin.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character; worms rarely act on the dreamer, so the coding usually rests on emotion and any misfortune involved.
lenses.modern: Worm dreams often follow gardening or rain; when they disturb, continuity suggests looking for a worry that feels as if it is eating at you.

reflect: What in my life is quietly turning into fertile ground?
What worry is eating away at me from inside?
Where do I make myself small?

name: Writing
aliases: words keep changing as i write
summary: Writing in dreams is about expression and record: putting thoughts into words, communicating, or trying to fix something before it slips away.
meaning: Dream writing ranges from fluent pages to pens that run dry and words that rearrange themselves. Fluent writing can reflect clarity, creativity or something you are ready to say; struggling to write may mirror difficulty expressing a feeling, or fear that your words will be misread. Notice what you were writing and for whom. A letter suggests a message meant for a specific person; a book, a larger story about your life; a list, the need to hold everything together. If you wake with a phrase from the dream, write it down.

contexts.reading: Clarity or creative energy; a good moment to put something into words by day too.
Blocked expression; ask what you are hesitant to say, or to whom.
A message waiting to be delivered, or a conversation you want to have.

lenses.freud: Freud read words in dreams closely, treating them as condensed and displaced material whose sound and shape could carry hidden meanings.
lenses.jung: Writing can picture the ego recording messages from the unconscious; Jung himself kept careful written and painted records of his inner images.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an activity, with the written item (a letter, a book) coded as a communication object.
lenses.modern: Keeping a written dream journal tends to improve dream recall over time, which is why it is so widely recommended.

reflect: What am I trying to put into words?
Whom was I writing to?
What phrase from the dream do I still remember?

name: Younger Self
summary: Your younger self often brings back earlier needs, hopes and hurts, inviting you to see where they still live in you.
meaning: When you meet yourself as a child or teenager, or find yourself young again, the dream often points to something from that time that still matters: a need that was not met, a dream you set aside, a joy you lost touch with. The emotion is the key. A happy younger self may be inviting play and freedom back into your life. A frightened, lonely or ignored one may show a tender part of you that needs the care you can now give. Talking with your younger self can be a powerful moment of self-compassion.

contexts.when: You are young again and carefree
contexts.reading: Often a longing for freedom or play; what could you bring back into adult life?

contexts.when: Your younger self is sad or frightened
contexts.reading: A tender need may be surfacing; how would you comfort that child now?

contexts.when: You talk with your younger self
contexts.reading: A meeting of past and present; notice what each of you needed to say.

lenses.freud: Freud held that dreams draw on childhood experiences; a Freudian reading looks for childhood wishes still alive beneath present concerns.
lenses.jung: The younger self can carry the child archetype: vulnerability and renewal, the promise of what can still develop.
lenses.hvdc: The dreamer is not counted as a character; a child seen from outside may simply be coded as a child character, while the meaning comes from your report.
lenses.modern: Dreams recombine old and recent memories; younger-self dreams often surface when present events echo earlier experiences.

reflect: How old were you in the dream?
What did that younger you need?
How can you meet that need today?

name: Zebra
summary: The zebra is often read as individuality within a group, a balance of opposites, black and white, and the safety of the herd.
meaning: Every zebra's stripes are unique, yet zebras survive by staying together, so the image can speak of being yourself within a group. Black and white stripes also suggest opposites in balance, or black-and-white thinking, where things seem either right or wrong with nothing in between. A zebra standing out among horses may reflect feeling different. A herd moving as one can mirror the comfort of belonging, or the pull to blend in.

contexts.reading: Feeling different or noticed; consider whether that is uncomfortable or freeing.
Safety in numbers, belonging, or the pressure to blend in.
Black-and-white thinking; the dream may invite a more nuanced view.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the stripes as condensation: opposite wishes, to belong and to stand out, held in one image.
lenses.jung: Jung's attention to the union of opposites suits the zebra: light and dark side by side, contradictions held rather than resolved.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as an animal character, a herd as a group; most zebra dreams are coded by setting and emotion, with little interaction.
lenses.modern: Zebra dreams often accompany questions of identity and belonging, the brain borrowing a striking image to process standing out.

reflect: Where do I want to stand out, and where to blend in?
What am I seeing in black and white?
What makes my stripes my own?

name: Zombie
summary: Zombies are often read as numbness, routine on autopilot, or pressure from a crowd that seems to have lost its individuality.
meaning: Zombie dreams are rarely about death; they are about life without spark. The slow, relentless crowd can mirror demands that keep coming whatever you do, or a sense that people around you are going through the motions. Sometimes the zombie is you: tired, numb, moving through days without feeling. Surviving an outbreak can reflect resourcefulness under pressure. Films and games often supply the image; the feeling usually comes from waking life.

contexts.when: A crowd of zombies closes in
contexts.reading: Relentless demands, or social pressure that feels faceless.
Exhaustion or numbness; perhaps a cue to rest and seek what brings you back to life.
Resourcefulness and resilience under pressure.

lenses.freud: In the spirit of Freud's essay on the uncanny (1919), the zombie is the familiar made strange: people we know, emptied of life.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the zombie as the persona without soul, the risk of a life lived only in routine, cut off from feeling.
lenses.hvdc: Coded as imaginary characters, usually a group, in the Dead and Imaginary class; a chase is coded as aggression toward the dreamer.
lenses.modern: Zombie dreams fit threat simulation (Revonsuo 2000); fiction supplies the image, while waking overload or numbness often supplies the feeling.

reflect: Where am I living on autopilot?
What demands keep coming whatever I do?
What brings me back to life?

name: Zoo
summary: A zoo is wildness on display behind bars, often read as instincts or feelings held in check, observed safely, or ready to escape.
meaning: At a zoo, wild animals live within fences while people watch. Dreams set there often concern the instincts and emotions you keep contained: anger, desire, playfulness, fear. Walking calmly past enclosures may reflect a comfortable distance from your wilder side. Animals escaping can mirror feelings breaking loose; animals unhappy in small cages, a sense that something natural in you is too confined. Being inside a cage yourself suggests feeling watched or restricted. Which animal drew you may matter most.

contexts.reading: You may be observing your instincts from a safe distance.
A feeling you usually contain may be breaking free.
Something natural in you may feel too confined.

lenses.freud: A Freudian reading might see the caged animals as drives held back by the ego, and their escape as the return of what was repressed.
lenses.jung: A Jungian reading might see the animals as instinctual parts of the psyche, and ask how to relate to them rather than cage them.
lenses.hvdc: A zoo is coded as an outdoor setting; each kind of animal present is coded as an animal character.
lenses.modern: Animal characters are more common in children's dreams than in adults'; for an adult, a zoo may mirror how waking emotions are contained.

reflect: Which animal caught your attention, and how did it seem?
Were the cages keeping you safe, or keeping something in?
Which instinct in you needs more room?
